result.question: Adversarial prior-art / novelty gate on one claim set from an unpublished paper. Instrument: a deterministic self-feeding loop over a language model, x_{t+1} = argmax p(x | x_{t-1}, x_t), iterated from 96 random two-token starts; readouts are the FIXED-POINT FRACTION and a four-way fixed-point CLASS (funnel / none / fragmented / borderline). The companion published paper (arXiv:2608.10986) already covers the instrument and an instruction-tuning null. The claims to check are all about the DOMAIN — the tokens conditioning the model BEFORE the loop starts (nothing / BOS / ordinary text / chat template / high-markup structural text): C1 the domain dominates the readouts (flips the class, the model ranking at Spearman +0.400/+0.300 vs a 0.6 concordance gate, and the scalar — more than instruction tuning does; nine tokens move fixed-point fraction 0.21->0.98 or 0.71->0.01; a single BOS token 0.21->0.91). C2 it is not a length effect (non-monotone in prefix token count: 0.948 -> 0.005 -> 1.000 -> 0.000 across 0/1/9/9 tokens). C3 direction is not fixed — on models with headroom both ways, most conditioning reduces structure but some models move both ways depending only on which prefix is used. C4 (central) the effect is not a property of the prefix — ONE fixed 9-token Pile table-of-contents fragment raises two models to ~1.0 and drives four others to ~0.0, so no prefix can be certified "safe" or "structure-raising" independent of the weights; effects are OPPOSITE across models, not merely unshared. C5 (methodological) recurring failure of "a criterion with a shape applied to a quantity with no room to vary" (floor/ceiling makes a test unable to fail), plus confident universals from n=2 dying at n=9. Sub-questions: (a) does prior work show pre-loop conditioning / prompt scaffold dominates the readouts of iterative or self-feeding LM probes (self-consistency, self-refine, iterated refinement, agentic loops, Markov-chain-like text resampling) — i.e. probe output as scaffold artifact rather than model property? (b) does the large prompt-format-robustness literature ever measure FIXED-POINT, ATTRACTOR or CYCLE structure of the model's own greedy/argmax map under varying prefixes (as opposed to accuracy, sampled-output diversity, calibration), and does any of it report model RANKING INSTABILITY under prompt-format change (which would partly pre-empt C1)? (c) does any prior work report the SAME prefix having OPPOSITE-SIGNED effects on different models for a STRUCTURAL, non-accuracy property — possibly known as prompt-model interaction, prompt transferability failure, non-transferable prompts (sharpest form of C4)? (d) does the neural text degeneration / repetition-loop literature (Holtzman et al. and successors) systematically vary the PREFIX and report model-specific dependence, and does anyone census fixed points of greedy decoding at all? (e) is there prior work arguing prompt effects on a structural property are UNPREDICTABLE IN PRINCIPLE / cannot be corrected for — arguing against calibration rather than proposing one? (f) BOS-specific: work on the beginning-of-sequence token's effect on decoding dynamics, attention sinks, or fixed-point structure? VERDICT: for EACH of C1-C4 separately — novel, partially anticipated, or already taken — naming the 3-6 most threatening papers with citations and stating which claim each threatens and how much of it. If C4 is already known under another name, surface that first and plainly.
result.summary: The claim set has one structural spine (a prefix, not the weights, controls a dynamical readout, with model-dependent sign) that could be pre-empted from five separate literatures that rarely cite each other. So each angle targets a different community that could already own a piece of C1-C4 — iterated/self-feeding LM loops, prompt-format robustness and ranking instability, prompt-model interaction and transferability failure (the C4 killer), greedy-decoding degeneration and repetition attractors, and BOS/attention-sink mechanics — rather than re-searching the same phrasing five ways.

angles.label: iterative/self-feeding probes as scaffold artifact (sub-question a)
angles.query: iterated self-feeding language model loop fixed point attractor greedy argmax map prompt scaffold artifact self-refine self-consistency dynamical system arXiv
angles.rationale: Targets sub-question (a) and the closest instrument analogues: LLM-as-iterated-map / self-refine / self-consistency / Markov-chain text resampling work. A paper here showing loop outputs are driven by the prompt scaffold rather than the weights would hit C1 directly and is the most likely home for an existing fixed-point census.

angles.label: prompt-format robustness and model RANKING instability (sub-questions b, e)
angles.query: prompt format sensitivity language models leaderboard ranking flips Spearman correlation formatting perturbation spread irreducible cannot be calibrated
angles.rationale: Covers the large formatting-robustness literature. Two specific hits matter: papers reporting that model rankings reorder under prompt-format change (partially pre-empts C1's ranking claim), and papers arguing the variance is irreducible / not correctable (would pre-empt C5's stance in (e)). Also checks whether any of them measure attractor structure instead of accuracy.

angles.label: same prompt, opposite sign across models — the C4 threat (sub-question c)
angles.query: same prompt opposite effect across different models prompt-model interaction effect non-transferable prompts prompt transferability failure sign reversal structural property
angles.rationale: The single highest-stakes angle: C4 is the central claim and is the one most likely already named (prompt-model interaction, prompt transferability failure, negative transfer of prompts). Deliberately phrased around effect direction/sign reversal for a non-accuracy property, so it does not just return prompt-tuning-transfer accuracy results.

angles.label: greedy decoding degeneration, repetition attractors, prefix dependence (sub-question d)
angles.query: neural text degeneration repetition loop greedy decoding prefix conditioning model-specific attractor self-reinforcement Holtzman follow-up analysis
angles.rationale: Sub-question (d): the degeneration literature already studies where deterministic decoding gets stuck (repetition loops are fixed points/cycles by another name). Need to know whether anyone systematically varies the prefix and reports model-specific dependence — that would threaten C2/C3 and part of C1 — and whether any census of greedy fixed points already exists.

angles.label: BOS token, attention sinks, first-token effects on decoding dynamics (sub-question f)
angles.query: beginning-of-sequence BOS token attention sink effect language model decoding dynamics entropy first token presence ablation streaming
angles.rationale: Sub-question (f): the 0.21 -> 0.91 single-BOS result is the most quotable datum in C1 and the attention-sink literature is the adjacent field most likely to have already shown that adding/removing BOS qualitatively changes downstream generation behavior. Ablation and streaming-LLM studies are the specific risk.

results.title: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr — Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design (FormatSpread), ICLR 2024
results.snippet: THE most threatening paper for C1's ranking component and for (e). Semantically-equivalent format changes (separators, casing, spacing) produce "performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points" on LLaMA-2-13B, and critically: "format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen fixed prompt format." That sentence is the accuracy-domain version of C1's ranking claim AND a weak version of C4 (the same format is not good/bad across weights) — already published, 2023. Their stance also partly occupies (e): they do not propose a calibration or a canonical format; they argue the right move is to REPORT an interval of expected performance across sampled formats, i.e. treat the spread as an irreducible property of the evaluation rather than something to correct. What it does NOT do: it measures task ACCURACY only, never a structural/dynamical property, never fixed points, attractors, cycles, or any iterated/self-feeding map. Verdict contribution: C1 partially anticipated (ranking instability + weak cross-model correlation of prefix effects); C4 partially anticipated only in the weak "not shared" form, NOT the strong opposite-sign form the paper claims. Related negative result worth recording: an arXiv abstract search for "fixed point" AND "greedy decoding" returns ZERO papers, and no paper in the format-robustness literature censuses attractor structure of the argmax map — the attractor work that does exist (2502.15208 successive paraphrasing 2-period cycles; 2606.30571 multi-turn attractor states) is a disjoint literature that does not treat the prefix as the independent variable.

results.title: Alzahrani et al. — When Benchmarks are Targets: Revealing the Sensitivity of Large Language Model Leaderboards (ACL 2024)
results.snippet: Direct prior art for the RANKING half of C1. Minor, semantically-innocuous perturbations to benchmark presentation (changing answer-choice order/labels, single-token perturbations to MMLU-style items) "result in changes in rankings up to 8 positions" on the Open LLM Leaderboard. Same weights, same items, only the surrounding scaffold varies — the exact logical structure of C1's "varying only the prefix reorders models." So the claim "model ranking is not invariant to conditioning text" is NOT novel as a general proposition; what remains potentially novel in C1 is that the reordered quantity is a dynamical readout (fixed-point fraction) rather than an accuracy score, and that the reordering is quantified against a concordance gate (Spearman +0.400/+0.300 vs 0.6). Recommend the paper explicitly cite this and narrow C1 to the structural-readout scope, or a reviewer will read C1's ranking sentence as re-derivation. Note their remedy is a hybrid scoring method plus best-practice recommendations, so they sit on the CORRECTABLE side of (e), i.e. they do not pre-empt an anti-calibration stance.

results.title: Voronov, Wolf, Ryabinin — Mind Your Format: Towards Consistent Evaluation of In-Context Learning Improvements (ACL Findings 2024)
results.snippet: Threatens C4 and C3 harder than anything else in the format literature. Two results: (1) "a poor choice of the template can reduce the performance of the strongest models to a random guess level" — a huge, non-graded response to a purely presentational change; (2) "the best templates do not transfer between different setups and even between models of the same family." (2) is prompt-model interaction stated plainly and at scale, which is precisely the mechanism C4 asserts. The gap C4 can still claim: non-transfer of the OPTIMUM is weaker than OPPOSITE-SIGNED effects of a single fixed prefix (their finding is "the ranking of templates differs by model," not "one template pushes model A to the ceiling and model B to the floor"). C4's strong form — same 9-token prefix drives two models to ~1.0 and four to ~0.0 — is not stated here, but a reviewer will ask why it is more than an instance of known prompt-model interaction. They also propose Template Ensembles as a mitigation, so they oppose the (e) stance.

results.title: Cao, Cai, Zhang, Zou, Lam — On the Worst Prompt Performance of Large Language Models (NeurIPS 2024)
results.snippet: Best available prior art for sub-question (e) — the closest thing to an argument that the variance is not correctable. Reports "a difference of 45.48% between the worst and best performance for the Llama-2-70B-chat model" across semantically-equivalent task-level prompts, and its headline negative results are the anti-calibration ones: it emphasizes "the difficulty in identifying the worst prompt from both model-agnostic and model-dependent perspectives," and finds that existing prompt-engineering and prompt-consistency methods have only limited impact on worst-case performance. So the posture "you cannot certify a prompt as safe in advance, and known corrections do not close the gap" is already in print for accuracy. This partially pre-empts the epistemic framing behind C4 ("prefixes cannot be certified as safe or structure-raising independent of the model") — recommend citing it as the accuracy-domain precedent and positioning C4 as the structural-domain analogue with an explicit sign reversal, which they do not show.

results.title: Lu, Bartolo, Moore, Riedel, Stenetorp — Fantastically Ordered Prompts and Where to Find Them (ACL 2022)
results.snippet: The foundational non-transferability citation, and old enough (2021) that omitting it looks like a literature gap. Permuting only the ORDER of in-context examples — no content change at all — spans "the difference between near state-of-the-art and random guess performance," and the key line for C4: "a given good permutation for one model is not transferable to another." This establishes prompt-model interaction as known since 2021, meaning C4 cannot be framed as discovering that prefix effects are model-dependent; it can only claim the sharper sign-reversal form and the structural (non-accuracy) readout. Mitigating factor for the paper: they DO propose a fix (entropy statistics over candidate permutations to select performant orderings), so they sit on the correctable side and do not pre-empt (e); and order-permutation is a different manipulation from a fixed pre-loop prefix.

results.title: Kostiuk & Enevoldsen — One prompt is not enough: Instruction Sensitivity Undermines Embedding Model Evaluation (2026)
results.snippet: The most extreme published statement of ranking instability, and recent (May 2026) so it postdates most of the above: "the leaderboard ranking is not robust to prompt selection: a developer can improve their rank by favorably selecting prompts, and under adversarial prompt selection any model can be promoted to first place." If any model can be made rank-1 by prefix choice alone, then C1's ranking result (Spearman +0.400/+0.300 failing a 0.6 concordance gate) is a mild instance of an already-documented and stronger phenomenon — flag this as the single biggest threat to C1's ranking framing after Alzahrani. Domain caveat that preserves some novelty: this is embedding-model retrieval evaluation with instruction prefixes, not generative decoding dynamics, and the measured quantity is a task metric, not a dynamical readout. Their recommendation (evaluate over multiple prompts, report sensitivity alongside point estimates) again lands on the mitigable side of (e). Method note for the parent: WebSearch quota was exhausted this session, so this sweep ran through arXiv API abstract queries — coverage of non-arXiv venues (TACL/CL journal, workshop proceedings) is untested and the (e) axis in particular deserves one more pass, since no paper found argues prompt-induced variance is unpredictable IN PRINCIPLE; the strongest available is Cao et al.'s empirical "existing mitigations do not work."

results.title: Scaffolding the Strategist: Architecture-Dependent Reasoning Interventions in Hotelling Spatial Markets (Singh, 2026)
results.snippet: THE SHARPEST DIRECT ANALOGUE TO C4, and it uses the canonical name: "a significant crossover interaction: commitment scaffolding improves the standard model (+0.21) while degrading the reasoning model (-0.63), and principled separation shows the opposite pattern (-0.40 vs +0.31)" (t(7)=4.79, p=0.002, d=1.69). One fixed prompt scaffold, opposite-signed effects across two models, statistically tested and named. THREAT: C4's *structure* (same prefix, opposite sign, so prefixes cannot be certified model-independently) is already reported and already has a name -- 'crossover interaction'. LIMIT: only n=2 models, and the measured quantity is judged task performance on strategic reasoning, NOT a structural/dynamical property. So it pre-empts the CONCEPT but not the DOMAIN of C4. The paper's own framing (interventions must be evaluated per-architecture, not certified globally) is close enough to C4's 'cannot certify a prefix as safe' that the paper should be cited and distinguished explicitly.

results.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design (FormatSpread; Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr, 2023)
results.snippet: The canonical prompt-format-sensitivity paper, and the biggest threat to C1's RANKING sub-claim. Verified quote from the abstract: "We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format." THREAT: (i) C1's model-ranking-instability-under-prefix component is substantially anticipated -- ranking flips under formatting are established; (ii) partially anticipates C4, since weak cross-model correlation of format effects is the aggregate statistic C4 dramatizes at the level of individual prefixes. IMPORTANT DISTINCTION TO PRESERVE: 'weakly correlated' is NOT 'opposite-signed'; Sclar et al. report non-shared effects, not sign reversal, and the measured quantity is task accuracy, not fixed-point structure. C1 should be rewritten to concede ranking instability as prior art and claim novelty only for the readout being a structural class/attractor statistic.

results.title: Does Your VFM Speak Plant? The Botanical Grammar of Vision Foundation Models for Object Detection (Lundqvist et al., 2026)
results.snippet: Verified abstract sentence: "Models respond divergently to prompt structure: conditions that optimize one architecture can collapse another." Four open-vocabulary detectors, one prompt-dimension grid -- a prompt that maximizes one architecture drives another to collapse. This is C4's exact sentence shape ('raises two models to ~1.0, drives four others to ~0.0') transplanted to vision. THREAT: shows the 'prefixes cannot be certified model-independently' conclusion is already drawn in an adjacent modality, so C4 cannot be presented as a conceptually unprecedented finding. MITIGATION: it is vision-language object detection measured by detection accuracy (mAP-type), not autoregressive decoding dynamics, and it does not measure any iterated-map or fixed-point property.

results.title: Mind Your Format: Towards Consistent Evaluation of In-Context Learning Improvements (Voronov, Wolf, Ryabinin, 2024)
results.snippet: Verified abstract claim: "the best templates do not transfer between different setups and even between models of the same family." Directly pre-empts the weaker reading of C4 -- that a prefix's effect is a property of the model+prefix pair rather than of the prefix -- and reinforces the C1 threat alongside FormatSpread. NOTE FOR THE VERDICT: I asked specifically whether the paper reports directional reversal, and it does not; it reports inconsistency in which template is best, not that one template moves two models in opposite directions from the same baseline. This is exactly the 'not merely unshared' distinction C4 is built on, so this paper is the best foil for sharpening C4's wording: prior work establishes non-transfer, C4 would claim anti-transfer.

results.title: General-purpose LLMs as Models of Human Driver Behavior: The Case of Simplified Merging (Mohammad, Mooi, Zgonnikov, 2026)
results.snippet: Prompt-ablation study across OpenAI o3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro concluding that "prompt components act as model-specific inductive biases that do not transfer across LLMs." Relevant because the measured property is BEHAVIORAL/DYNAMICAL (control patterns, tactical response to spatial vs velocity cues, safety outcomes) rather than benchmark accuracy -- the closest I found to a non-accuracy property whose prompt dependence is declared model-specific. THREAT: moderate; it narrows the 'nobody has shown this for a non-accuracy property' defense of C4. LIMIT: I confirmed the abstract does not report opposite-signed effects of an identical prompt component across the two models -- it reports differential sensitivity and divergent safety performance, which is C4's weaker cousin.

results.title: PromptBridge: Cross-Model Prompt Transfer for Large Language Models (2025)
results.snippet: Names the phenomenon 'Model Drifting': a prompt engineered for one LLM "yields substantially worse performance" on another, motivating an explicit cross-model mapping. Included specifically because the parent asked whether C4 is 'already known under a different name' -- this is one of the names (alongside 'crossover interaction', 'prompt-model interaction effect', and the older prompt-tuning-transfer line: SPoT 2110.07904, On Transferability of Prompt Tuning 2111.06719, Zero-Shot Continuous Prompt Transfer 2310.01691). THREAT: naming/framing only. Model Drifting is a degradation claim (transfer makes things worse), which is a one-sided, accuracy-scoped version of C4; it does not claim sign reversal and does not touch structural readouts. C4 should cite it to show awareness and then distinguish anti-transfer from mere drift.

results.title: When LLMs Play the Telephone Game: Cultural Attractors as Conceptual Tools to Evaluate LLMs (Perez et al., 2024)
results.snippet: THE BIGGEST THREAT IN THIS LANE, and it threatens C1 directly. Iterated transmission chains are a self-feeding loop, and the abstract states they "uncover the existence of biases and attractors, and study their dependence on the initial text, the instructions, language model, and model size." That is already a factorial INITIAL-TEXT x INSTRUCTION x MODEL design over attractor properties of an iterated LM loop — i.e. someone has already asked whether the pre-loop conditioning or the weights dominates attractor structure. They also report that "more open-ended instructions lead to stronger attraction effects compared to more constrained tasks," a prompt-dominates-the-readout result in kind if not in metric. Differences from the claim set: their attractors are text-property attractors (toxicity, length, positivity) measured over sampled chains, not fixed points of a deterministic argmax map, and no fixed-point fraction or four-way class label. CRITICAL FULL-TEXT CHECK: whether their per-model breakdown shows the same initial text moving attractor strength in OPPOSITE directions across models. If it does, C4 is substantially anticipated under the name "initial-text dependence of cultural attractors." The abstract alone does not report opposite-signed interactions.

results.title: Unveiling Attractor Cycles in Large Language Models: A Dynamical Systems View of Successive Paraphrasing (Wang, Li, Yan, Cheng, Zhang, 2025)
results.snippet: Closest published instrument to the probe itself, and it contains a sentence that cuts against C1 rather than for it. Successive paraphrasing is an explicit self-feeding loop analyzed as a dynamical system; they report convergence to "stable periodic states, such as 2-period attractor cycles," attributed to "the self-reinforcing nature of LLMs." Decisive line for the gate: "This pattern persists with increasing generation randomness or alternating prompts and LLMs." So prompt variation was already tried on an iterated-loop attractor readout and reported as NOT changing the qualitative structure. This is a double-edged result: it weakens any claim that iterated-loop-plus-attractor-census is a new instrument (that is now prior art), but it makes C1 a direct empirical CONTRADICTION of a published robustness claim rather than a restatement of it — which is a stronger novelty position, provided the paper cites and engages it. Note the readout is cycle periodicity over sampled paraphrases, not fixed-point fraction of an argmax map, and no cross-model ranking or Spearman concordance is computed.

results.title: Learning to Break the Loop: Analyzing and Mitigating Repetitions for Neural Text Generation (Xu, Liu, Yan, Cai, Li, Li, 2022)
results.snippet: The canonical Holtzman successor that establishes CONTEXT DOMINANCE over deterministic looping, so it partially pre-empts the mechanism behind C1 and C2's non-monotonicity. Core finding: "language models have a preference to repeat the previous sentence" and "sentence-level repetitions have a self-reinforcement effect: the more times a sentence is repeated in the context, the higher the probability of continuing to generate that sentence." That is a quantified, monotone dependence of loop-entry probability on what is in the pre-generation context — the degeneration field already knows the prefix controls whether the deterministic map falls into a repetition attractor. What it does NOT do, and where C1-C4 keep room: no census over many random starts, no fixed-point FRACTION as a scalar readout, no discrete class label, no model RANKING under prefix change, and no report of the same context driving different models in opposite directions. Its self-reinforcement result is also monotone in repeat count, which is the opposite shape from C2's non-monotone 0.948 -> 0.005 -> 1.000 -> 0.000 in prefix length; C2 is not anticipated here.

results.title: Consistency of a Recurrent Language Model With Respect to Incomplete Decoding (Welleck, Kulikov, Kim, Pang, Cho, 2020)
results.snippet: The formal precedent for treating greedy decoding as a map that can fail to halt. Proves that "greedy search, beam search, top-k sampling, and nucleus sampling" are inconsistent — they can produce infinite-length sequences with zero probability under the model — and demonstrates this empirically, then proposes self-terminating models (extended by Choi, Cho, Lee, arXiv:2210.00660). This is the nearest thing in the literature to a structural statement about where the deterministic decoding map ends up, and it is the strongest available answer to "does anyone census fixed points of greedy decoding at all?" ANSWER: no full census exists. Welleck et al. characterize non-termination as a possibility class, not as a per-model measured fraction over randomized starts, and the prefix is not a manipulated variable. Combined with Holtzman et al. (arXiv:1904.09751), which uses a fixed WebText prefix set and never varies it as an independent variable, this leaves the fixed-point-fraction census and the four-way class label uncontested in the degeneration literature.

results.title: What LLMs Think When You Don't Tell Them What to Think About? (Kwon and Zou, 2026)
results.snippet: Threatens C3's model-specificity framing and the empty/minimal-prefix condition specifically. Runs 16 LLMs across families (GPT-OSS, Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen) on minimal, topic-neutral inputs — the nearest published analogue to the nothing/BOS end of the domain ladder — and reports that "the near-unconstrained generation often degenerates into repetitive phrases, revealing interesting behaviors unique to each model family," with sharply divergent per-family attractor content (GPT-OSS 27.1% programming / 24.6% math; Qwen multiple-choice questions; DeepSeek religious text). 256k released samples. So "degeneration under near-empty conditioning is model-specific" is already on record. What it does not establish: it varies the model at fixed minimal prompt rather than varying the prefix at fixed model, measures topical content rather than fixed-point structure, and reports no sign reversal of a scalar structural quantity. C4's opposite-direction result is not touched; C3 is weakened to "already suspected, now quantified on a structural readout."

results.title: Attractor States Emerge in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations (Ko and Geiping, 2026)
results.snippet: Relevant as the strongest published statement of the position C1 attacks, so it is a foil the paper should name. Self-play conversation is a self-feeding loop; across 7 LLMs and 20 controversial topics they find "model-specific attractors" that are "topic-independent stable sets of behaviors," tracked in representation space, plus asymmetric influence in mixed-play ("Claude Haiku is a strong attractor of other models in latent space"; GPT-4.1 nano "especially malleable"). The explicit claim is that attractor identity is a property of the WEIGHTS and is invariant to the conditioning topic — i.e. published evidence for domain-does-not-matter. That makes C1 a contested empirical claim rather than an unexamined one, and it supplies a ready reviewer objection ("topic-independence is already established") that must be answered by pointing at the distinction between semantic topic variation and structural markup/scaffold variation. Also note the per-model asymmetry (strong attractor vs malleable) is a model-specific SUSCEPTIBILITY result, which is C3-adjacent but not C4: no single conditioning input is shown to push two models in opposite directions.

results.title: When LLMs Play the Telephone Game: Cultural Attractors as Conceptual Tools to Evaluate LLMs in Multi-turn Settings (Perez et al., v4 2026-01-29)
results.snippet: THE MOST THREATENING PAPER ON THIS ANGLE for C1. A true iterated self-feeding loop (transmission chain: LLM output becomes the next LLM's input), analyzed explicitly in terms of 'biases and attractors', and — critically — it already asks the domain question: it studies 'their dependence on the initial text, the instructions, language model, and model size'. Headline result is a conditioning effect: 'more open-ended instructions lead to stronger attraction effects compared to more constrained tasks.' This partially anticipates C1's GENRE (pre-loop conditioning modulates the attractor readout of an iterated LM probe, across models). What it does NOT do: readouts are semantic text properties (toxicity, positivity, difficulty, length), not a fixed-point fraction of a deterministic argmax map; no census over random starts; no discrete class label; no ranking of models; and no claim of OPPOSITE-SIGNED effects of one fixed prefix across models — so C4 is untouched. Verdict contribution: C1 partially anticipated at the level of 'conditioning matters', novel at the level of 'dominates a fixed-point census and flips model ranking'.

results.title: Unveiling Attractor Cycles in Large Language Models: A Dynamical Systems View of Successive Paraphrasing (v2 2025-05-16)
results.snippet: The closest published INSTRUMENT analogue: LLM framed as a map that 'iteratively maps input text to output text', analyzed for 'attractors, including fixed points and limit cycles', converging to '2-period attractor cycles'. This is the paper a reviewer will cite against the instrument's framing novelty (the companion paper arXiv:2608.10986 needs to engage it). But for the DOMAIN claim set it is a foil rather than a pre-emption, and a useful one: it explicitly reports the attractor pattern 'persists with increasing generation randomness or ALTERNATING PROMPTS and LLMs' — i.e. it looked at prompt variation and concluded prompt does NOT change the qualitative structure. C1 is the direct contradiction of that sentence, which makes C1 novel but also raises the bar: the paper must explain why the argmax-map fixed-point census is prefix-dominated where successive paraphrasing was prefix-robust. Note the level mismatch: this operates at the semantic paraphrase level with sampling, not a short-window deterministic token-level argmax map.

results.title: Do Language Models Converge to Themselves? Recursive Self-Refinement as Textual Relaxation (2026-06-26)
results.snippet: Nearest vocabulary collision: recursive refinement as 'a dynamical process in which repeated LLM revision drives text toward a model-preferred soft fixed-point region', measuring 'exact and approximate fixed points' and noting 'deterministic decoding reaches exact fixed points earlier'. So 'fixed point of an iterated LM loop' is established terminology as of mid-2026 and cannot be claimed as new. It pre-empts NONE of C1-C4: single model (GPT-5.5), fixed seeded inputs (50 ICML abstracts) rather than random starts, no prefix/conditioning variation, no fixed-point FRACTION over a start census, no cross-model ranking, no BOS or chat-template treatment. Also the load-bearing NEGATIVE from this angle: a targeted arXiv sweep for enumeration/census of fixed points of the greedy/argmax next-token map, and for prefix-dependent greedy-decoding degeneration structure, returned this paper and zero true matches — the fixed-point-fraction census over random two-token starts appears unoccupied.

results.title: Attractor States Emerge in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations (2026-06-29)
results.snippet: Relevant to C3/C4's framing rather than to C1. Across 7 LLMs and 20 topics it finds 'self-play trajectories to be model-specific attractors', with strongly asymmetric cross-model influence and large differences in malleability (Claude Haiku a strong attractor; GPT-4.1 nano 'especially malleable'). This establishes that MODEL-SPECIFIC attractor structure and heterogeneous per-model susceptibility to an external influence are already reported for a structural (non-accuracy) readout — which softens the surprise value of C3's 'direction is not fixed' and of C4's 'effects are model-dependent'. It does not reach C4's sharp form: the varied factor is the conversational partner, not a fixed pre-loop prefix, and no single fixed condition is shown driving some models to ~1.0 and others to ~0.0 on one scalar. Cite it pre-emptively; C4's 'opposite across weights from ONE fixed 9-token prefix' still looks unclaimed here.

results.title: Knowledge Collapse in LLMs: When Fluency Survives but Facts Fail under Recursive Synthetic Training (2025-09-05)
results.snippet: A self-consuming recursive loop whose outcome is reported as 'conditional, prompt-dependent', with INSTRUCTION FORMAT identified as a determinant of the collapse trajectory. This is the same shape of claim as C1 — the scaffold, not the weights, sets where the loop lands — but in the recursive-TRAINING setting rather than inference-time iterated decoding, and the readout is factual degradation rather than fixed-point structure. Threat level: it means 'the loop's outcome is governed by the conditioning format' is not a new idea in the abstract; the novelty of C1 must rest on the specific readouts (discrete class, model ranking, fixed-point fraction) and on the magnitudes (0.21 -> 0.98 from nine tokens). Does not touch C2 (non-monotonicity in prefix length), C3, or C4.

results.title: Sample More, Reflect Less: Self-Refine and Reflexion Lose to Repeated Sampling at Equal Token Cost, from 1.5B to 7B (2026-07-30)
results.snippet: Best example found of the 'iterative self-feeding probe output is a scaffold artifact, not a model property' argument in its accuracy-flavored form: at equalized token budget 'no method is reliably better than repeated sampling anywhere', with self-refinement 3.6-10.1 points BELOW the naive baseline at 7B. Useful as supporting citation for C5's methodological framing and for the general thesis that loop readouts index the harness rather than the weights. It pre-empts none of C1-C4 directly — the readout is task accuracy, the varied factor is the loop procedure and compute budget rather than the pre-loop prefix, and there is no fixed-point/attractor measurement. Adjacent MAGE (arXiv:2607.11944) documents a 'Prompt Optimization Coupling Effect' in the same spirit.

claims.claim: Minor, semantically-neutral format perturbations to a benchmark (answer-choice order, choice symbols, scoring method) reorder an 11-model leaderboard by up to 8 positions, with normalized Kendall's tau falling to 0.455-0.564 — i.e. model RANKING under a fixed set of weights and a fixed estimator is not stable to scaffold changes. This is the closest published pre-emption of the ranking-instability component of C1, but it is measured on task ACCURACY, not on a structural readout.
claims.quote: We show that for popular multiple-choice question benchmarks (e.g., MMLU), minor perturbations to the benchmark, such as changing the order of choices or the method of answer selection, result in changes in rankings up to 8 positions. [Table 1 caption:] The largest change in rank is 5 positions (Yi-6b) followed by 4 positions (Llama2-13b-chat). ... k_tau = 0.564 for this experiment, indicating a significant disagreement in rankings.

claims.claim: ONE fixed perturbation produces OPPOSITE-SIGNED effects across models, including within the same model family: fixing the correct answer at position A changes accuracy by +24.55 for Llama2-7b but -15.53 for Llama2-7b-chat, +1.41 for Yi-6b but -7.22 for Yi-34b, and the authors state explicitly that the favored position varies across models and within families. This is the C4 shape (same fixed scaffold, opposite direction across weights) already published — but for benchmark ACCURACY and position/token bias, not for a non-accuracy structural property such as fixed-point fraction.
claims.quote: All the LLMs tested showed a clear preference for specific positions/answer choice symbols, although the position varied among models and even in model families.

claims.claim: The authors argue these prompt/token effects change in UNPREDICTABLE ways and are difficult to mitigate — i.e. they argue against correctability rather than proposing a calibration — which is the shape of the C5/(e) methodological claim. Note the hedge: they say 'difficult to mitigate' and recommend a partial mitigation (hybrid scoring), not that the effect is uncorrectable in principle.
claims.quote: This experiment, displayed in Figure 6 and Table A.8, shows that (i) LLMs always bias toward the symbols representing the choice IDs and (ii) even after shuffling the symbols, bias changes in unpredictable ways. [Figure 6 caption:] Even using rare symbols, model selection bias changes unpredictably, indicating token and position bias are difficult to mitigate.

claims.claim: Crucially for the novelty gate, the perturbations that DID move rankings were to the answer choices and the scoring method — NOT to the pre-loop instruction prefix. Changes confined to the leading instruction/prompt text (removing the subject name, 'Correct Answer:' vs 'Answer:', trivial or out-of-domain few-shot examples) left rankings essentially intact at k_tau > 0.9. So this paper does not show that varying the PREFIX dominates the readout; it arguably shows the opposite for accuracy, which limits how much of C1 it pre-empts.
claims.quote: We also experiment with removing subject information from instructions and ending the prompt with "Correct Answer:" instead of "Answer:" (Figure 10, Tables A.20-A.23). We see little changes (k_tau > 0.9) in these prompt modification experiments.

claims.claim: The paper's entire measurement apparatus is a single-forward-pass log-likelihood comparison over four answer-letter tokens, scored with the LM Evaluation Harness; its only metrics are accuracy change (dAcc) and recall standard deviation (RStd, a selection-bias metric). It never iterates the model on its own output, and contains no measurement of greedy/argmax fixed points, attractors, cycles, or self-feeding dynamics, and no analysis of BOS or beginning-of-sequence tokens. It therefore cannot pre-empt the fixed-point/attractor structural readout in C1-C4, only the ranking-instability framing.
claims.quote: Their implementation of MMLU measures the log-likelihood of each of the answer tokens ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'] after the input prompt and chooses the letter with the highest probability as the model's answer. ... For each variation introduced to the MCQ benchmarks, we calculate the change in accuracy (dAcc) and recall standard deviation (RStd) for each model.

results.title: Why do LLMs attend to the first token? (Barbero, Arroyo, Gu, Perivolaropoulos, Bronstein, Veličković, Pascanu, 2025; arXiv:2504.02732)
results.snippet: THE SINGLE BIGGEST THREAT TO THE BOS DATUM IN C1. This paper does exactly the intervention the claim rests on — toggling ONE BOS token at inference — and reports large, qualitative, model-specific consequences. Full text: removing BOS from Gemma 7B drops ARC-e 80.77 -> 28.49, HellaSwag 80.61 -> 27.35, and the long-context Ruler benchmark 82.57 -> 0.00; with BOS fixed at position 1 during training, removing it at test time makes validation loss jump 2.69 -> 7.56. The mechanism offered is directly dynamical: the BOS sink is a brake on 'over-mixing', and without it 'representational distance to the mean decreases as prompt length increases', i.e. token representations collapse toward a uniform state — a contraction/attractor story in representation space. They also vary context length and data packing and find sink strength depends on both, and report family- and scale-dependent sink rates (LLaMa 3.1 8B 45.97% vs 405B 78.29%). VERDICT IMPACT: 'nine tokens / one BOS token change everything' is NOT novel as a phenomenon; what survives is the specific readout (fixed-point fraction of the iterated argmax map) and the opposite-sign-across-weights result. Note the shared author (Xiangming Gu) with the sink-emergence paper below — this is a coordinated line of work a reviewer will know.

results.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks (Xiao, Tian, Chen, Han, Lewis; ICLR 2024; arXiv:2309.17453)
results.snippet: The canonical prior art that the FIRST TOKEN dominates generation dynamics. Evicting the initial token's KV collapses window-attention perplexity and generation quality; 'keeping the KV of initial tokens will largely recover the performance of window attention.' They further propose training with a dedicated placeholder sink token. Threatens C1's BOS result at the level of 'the presence of one leading token is a first-order determinant of decoding behavior, not a second-order nuisance' — a reviewer will say this has been common knowledge since 2023. MITIGATION FOR THE PAPER: the mechanism here is KV-cache eviction under a modified (windowed) attention pattern, not prefix conditioning of an unmodified full-context model; the readout is perplexity/fluency, not a census of fixed points of the argmax map. So it pre-empts the framing, not the measurement.

results.title: When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models: An Empirical View (Gu, Pang, Du, Liu, Zhang, Du, Wang, Lin; ICLR 2025; arXiv:2410.10781)
results.snippet: Threatens the INTERPRETATION of the BOS result rather than the number, and does so in a way that could be used against C1/C2. Full-text ablations show the sink is POSITIONAL, not identity-based: re-sampling the first token uniformly from the vocabulary still yields a sink (27.03%), and fixing a token at position 2 or 3 during pre-training makes the sink 'always appear in the fixed token instead of the first token.' They also run unconditional generation with a BOS token 'fed into the model as the prefix', and note that when pre-training has no BOS the EOS is treated as one. Consequence for the claim set: a reviewer can argue the 0.21 -> 0.91 BOS jump is a generic first-position/prefix-slot effect already characterized here, and that the sink's dependence on 'loss function and data distribution' predicts model-to-model variation — which softens C3 and part of C4. They do NOT measure decoding fixed points or report opposite-signed effects across models.

results.title: Massive Activations in Large Language Models (Sun, Chen, Kolter, Liu; COLM 2024; arXiv:2402.17762)
results.snippet: Adjacent mechanism paper: a handful of activations ~100,000x larger than the rest, concentrated on the first token and on delimiter/low-semantic tokens, acting as 'indispensable bias terms' that 'largely stay constant regardless of the input.' Zeroing them catastrophically degrades the model. Two hooks into the claim set: (i) it supplies a ready-made mechanistic explanation for why one leading token flips global behavior, which weakens the surprise value of C1's BOS datum; (ii) WHICH token carries the massive activations varies by model — the closest thing in this literature to C4's 'the same prefix does different things to different weights', though here the variation is in the carrier token's identity rather than in the SIGN of an effect on a structural readout. Property measured is activation magnitude / loss, not a decoding-map property, so it does not take C4.

results.title: Attention Sinks in Diffusion Language Models (Rulli, Petruzzi, Michielon, Silvestri, Scardapane, Devoto; arXiv:2510.15731)
results.snippet: The closest published instance of an OPPOSITE-DIRECTION result for the same sink intervention, and therefore the sleeper threat to C4. Reports that diffusion LMs have DYNAMIC sink positions that move during generation and that they 'remain robust to sink removal, unlike autoregressive models' — i.e. one identical intervention (delete the sink) is catastrophic for one class of weights and a no-op for another. Caveats that keep C4 alive: the contrast is across ARCHITECTURE FAMILIES (diffusion vs autoregressive), not across same-family weights; and it is a robust/not-robust dichotomy rather than a genuinely signed reversal (raise to ~1.0 vs drive to ~0.0). If C4 gets challenged as 'already known', this is the paper a reviewer will reach for, so pre-empt it explicitly.

results.title: On the Existence and Behavior of Secondary Attention Sinks (Wong, Zhang, Mahon, Luk, Isopoussu, Zhao; arXiv:2512.22213)
results.snippet: Cross-model evidence that BOS-sink behavior is heterogeneous across weights: surveys 11 model families, finds the primary (BOS) sink weakens in middle layers while secondary sinks emerge, with multiple sink levels in larger models. Useful as the 'BOS effects are model-specific' prior art that partially blunts the novelty of C3 and the weaker reading of C4 (effects merely UNSHARED across models). It does not report effects of OPPOSITE SIGN on a single structural readout, which is the sharp form of C4 and appears to remain open. ALSO RECORD AS NEGATIVE EVIDENCE FOR THE GATE: a targeted arXiv full-text query for ('greedy decoding' AND 'fixed point') returns ZERO results, and the attention-sink corpus (40 top-relevance hits scanned) contains no census of fixed points/attractors of a model's own argmax map under varying prefixes — so the INSTRUMENT-level readout of C1/C2 looks unoccupied even though the BOS phenomenon itself does not.

claims.claim: Model-vs-model comparison outcomes reverse purely from changing the prompt format: with a fixed accuracy margin d=0.02, LLaMA-2-13B vs -70B reverse their ordering with probability 0.141, and LLaMA-2-7B vs Falcon-7B with probability 0.140. This is a direct, published instance of RANKING INSTABILITY of models under prefix/format change, and partially pre-empts the ranking component of C1 (though for task accuracy, not for a structural fixed-point readout).
claims.quote: Comparison trends between models are often reversed just by choosing different formats. ... Assuming model M is better than M′ by at least d accuracy using prompt p, we compute how often M′ achieves at least d higher accuracy than M under a different format p′. ... LLaMA-2-13B and -70B reverse trend by at least d= 0.02 with probability 0.141; LLaMA-2-7B and Falcon-7B reverse trend by at least d= 0.02 with probability 0.140.

claims.claim: The paper explicitly claims prompt formats have no model-independent valence — a format that is better than another under model M has less than 0.62 probability of retaining that ordering under a different model M′, and the authors state formats are 'not inherently good or bad'. This is the closest published analogue to C4's structure (same prefix, opposite-signed effect across weights), but it is asserted for accuracy ordering, and is framed as 'inconsistent/weakly correlated' rather than as a demonstrated sign REVERSAL of a structural quantity from a single fixed prefix.
claims.quote: Formats are not inherently good or bad. ... Table 2 shows that if format p1 has lower performance than format p2 under model M, there is <0.62 probability that this trend would hold under another model M′ ... findings of a format being better or worse than another are often inconsistent across models. ... formats yielding high performance for model M may not yield high performance for M′

claims.claim: Meaning-preserving, single-token-scale changes to the prompt scaffold produce very large swings in the measured readout: up to 76 accuracy points of spread on LLaMA-2-13B, and in one atomic case adding/removing a colon ('passage:{}' vs 'passage {}') moves accuracy from 0.043 to 0.826 (a 0.783 delta). This establishes prior art for the MAGNITUDE claim in C1 (small prefix edits dominating the readout), but for accuracy rather than fixed-point fraction.
claims.quote: with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B ... Table 1: Examples of atomic changes' impact on accuracy using probability ranking ... passage:{} | passage {} | 0.043 | 0.826 | 0.783

claims.claim: Every readout in the paper is downstream TASK PERFORMANCE (accuracy / probability-ranking accuracy over a task's label set); the paper measures no fixed-point, attractor, cycle, or iterated/self-feeding greedy-map property of the model, and does not census where deterministic argmax trajectories land. The instrument-level novelty of the claim set (fixed-point fraction and four-way fixed-point class as the thing the prefix moves) is therefore NOT pre-empted by this work.
claims.quote: we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights.

claims.claim: Format sensitivity is not eliminated by scale, more few-shot examples, or instruction tuning — parallel to the companion claim that instruction tuning does not change the class, and weakening any argument that the domain effect is an artifact of untuned models. Separately, the paper reports near-chance monotonicity when composing atomic format changes (32.4%/33.6% of triples monotonic vs 33.3% expected under random shuffling), which is an accuracy-domain analogue of C2's non-monotonicity but is about feature composition, not prefix LENGTH.
claims.quote: Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. ... 32.4 and 33.6% of triples were monotonic...random shuffling within a triple will result in monotonicity 33.3% of the time

claims.claim: A single fixed prompt scaffold produces statistically significant OPPOSITE-SIGNED effects on two different models: commitment scaffolding helps GPT-4.1-mini (+0.21) and hurts GPT-5-mini (-0.63), while principled separation reverses (-0.40 vs +0.31), with a crossover interaction at t(7)=4.79, p=0.002, d=1.69 and 7/8 directional consistency across questions. This establishes that 'same prompt, opposite sign across models' is already documented prior art in a rigorous statistical form — the generic phenomenon underlying C4 — under the name 'crossover interaction between scaffolding type and model architecture'.
claims.quote: We find a statistically significant crossover interaction between scaffolding type and model architecture ($t(7) = 4.79$, $p = 0.002$, $d = 1.69$): commitment scaffolding improves the standard model ($+0.21$) while degrading the reasoning model ($-0.63$), and principled separation shows the opposite pattern ($-0.40$ vs. $+0.31$). Both crossovers are individually significant (commitment: $p = 0.040$; separation: $p = 0.002$) and hold across all eight questions with 7/8 directional consistency.

claims.claim: The dependent variable is graded task performance on economics reasoning questions (720 human/LLM-judged responses scored for correctness of strategic reasoning), NOT any structural, dynamical, or non-accuracy property. The paper measures no fixed points, attractors, cycles, or equilibria of the model's own greedy/argmax map, so it does not pre-empt C4's specific claim about opposite-signed effects on a STRUCTURAL property.
claims.quote: we evaluate GPT-4.1-mini (a standard instruction-following model) and GPT-5-mini (a reasoning-optimized model) under five conditions - an unscaffolded baseline and four reasoning interventions - across eight questions spanning deductive and abductive reasoning, three prompt framings, and three repetitions per condition, yielding 720 individually judged responses.

claims.claim: The crossover result rests on exactly two models (n=2 architectures), one 'standard instruction-following' and one 'reasoning-optimized', so it cannot exhibit the many-model pattern C4 asserts (one prefix raising two models to ~1.0 while driving four others to ~0.0); it demonstrates sign reversal between two points, not opposite-signed partition of a six-model panel.
claims.quote: Using Hotelling's linear city model as a diagnostic vehicle, we evaluate GPT-4.1-mini (a standard instruction-following model) and GPT-5-mini (a reasoning-optimized model) under five conditions

claims.claim: The experimental design is single-pass prompt-and-judge (five conditions x eight questions x three framings x three repetitions), with no iterative, self-feeding, or self-refinement loop and no re-injection of model output as its own input; therefore it bears on sub-question (c) but says nothing about sub-question (a), pre-loop conditioning dominating iterative-probe readouts.
claims.quote: across eight questions spanning deductive and abductive reasoning, three prompt framings, and three repetitions per condition, yielding 720 individually judged responses

claims.claim: The paper frames the architecture-dependence as tractable and correctable — interventions can be matched to architectures rather than being unpredictable in principle — since one intervention fully repairs a documented deficit in one model while nothing helps the other. This is the opposite stance from C5/sub-question (e)'s 'cannot be corrected for' argument, so it does not pre-empt that claim.
claims.quote: We further document a persistent declarative-procedural gap in which both models identify correct strategies at rates far exceeding their ability to execute them; separation fully closes this gap for the reasoning model while no intervention helps the standard model.

claims.claim: Model RANKING on a leaderboard is not robust to prompt/instruction choice: across 6 embedding models and 11 datasets, adversarial prompt selection can promote ANY model in the study to rank 1, and a concrete non-adversarial example moves bge-large from rank 5 to rank 3. This is the closest published pre-emption of the RANKING half of C1 — but it is ranking on task-accuracy benchmarks, not ranking on a structural readout of an iterative argmax map.
claims.quote: under adversarial selection (an upper bound on manipulability), every model in our study can be promoted to rank 1 [...] bge-large rises from rank 5 to rank 3 under this configuration, overtaking e5-large [...] even a single model contributor optimizing their prompt, without any adversarial intent toward competitors, can distort the leaderboard

claims.claim: The instrument and measured quantity are entirely accuracy-based and non-dynamical: the objects studied are instruction EMBEDDING models (encoders with no autoregressive decode step), evaluated by task metrics (retrieval nDCG, classification accuracy, clustering) on MTEB-style datasets. No fixed point, attractor, cycle, greedy/argmax map, or any decoding-dynamics quantity is measured anywhere in the paper — so it cannot pre-empt the structural (fixed-point-fraction / fixed-point-class) content of C1-C4, only the generic 'prompts move rankings' framing.
claims.quote: Instruction embedding models have become common among state-of-the-art models, however are evaluated using a single prompt per task. [...] We present an empirical study of prompt sensitivity across 6 embedding models and 11 datasets.

claims.claim: The DIRECTION of the prompt effect is not fixed: relative to the distribution over plausible prompts, the default/reported prompt can systematically understate performance for some model-task pairs (BGE deflation example) and overstate it for others (Qwen3 on MIRACL inflation example). This is a bidirectional-effect result adjacent to C3, but it is stated over model-TASK pairs and different prompts, not as one fixed prefix producing opposite-signed movement across weights (C4).
claims.quote: The default prompt can both systematically understate or overstate performance. [...] the reported score is much lower that what would be expected [...] the default prompt produces an atypically strong result [...] most models report scores above the median of the prompt distribution

claims.claim: Sensitivity is model-specific, i.e. an interaction rather than a per-prompt constant: coefficients of variation over the prompt distribution reach 30-45% on individual tasks, and per-model score ranges over ~38-45 deduplicated prompts differ sharply by model (e.g. KaLM on AmazonCounterfactual 0.808-0.958, range 0.15, vs BGE-large on Touche2020 0.014-0.471, range 0.457). The paper documents unequal MAGNITUDE of prompt effect across models but never reports a single fixed prompt with OPPOSITE-SIGNED effects across models, so it does not take C4.
claims.quote: individual task CVs reach 30–45%, confirming that specific model–task combinations are highly sensitive

claims.claim: The paper argues FOR a correction, not against one: its prescription is multi-prompt evaluation or reporting a sensitivity statistic alongside the point estimate. It contains no in-principle unpredictability or non-correctability argument, so it does not pre-empt sub-question (e) or the C5 methodological claim — if anything it is the opposite stance (prompt effects are a measurable nuisance to be averaged over).
claims.quote: benchmarks should incorporate prompt robustness, either by evaluating over multiple prompts or by reporting sensitivity alongside point estimates [...] We recommend that benchmarks adopt multi-prompt evaluation or similar strategies to ensure that the reported rankings faithfully reflect the models' quality

claims.claim: Worst-case prompts do NOT transfer across models: the intersection of worst-performing paraphrases is ~2% for Llama-family models at k=1 (13% for Gemma) and "nearly zero" across all seven models tested, so a prompt cannot be certified good or bad independently of the weights. This is the closest published analogue to C4 — but the measured quantity is task win-rate, not a structural/dynamical readout, and the framing is "model-specific" (non-shared), NOT opposite-signed. It threatens C4's *logic* (no model-independent prompt certification) while leaving C4's specific structural, opposite-direction result standing.
claims.quote: even so, when k = 1 (considering only the worst prompt), the metric for Llama family models is only 2% (13% for Gemma), and less than 10% (20% for Gemma) when k = 2. Not to mention the results of all models are much lower, nearly zero. These results suggest that the prompts showcasing the lower-bound performance of the models are often model-specific.

claims.claim: Cross-model concordance of per-prompt performance rankings is quantified with Kendall's W (coefficient of concordance) and is low: W = 0.238 across all models (0.443 Llama family, 0.548 Gemma family, 0.401 mixed 7B), with 72.3% of cases at 'weak' agreement and only 2.1% 'strong'. The paper explicitly concludes model-independent characterization of prompts is unlikely. This pre-empts the *instrument* (a concordance gate on prompt/model rank agreement) used in C1's ranking argument, and is the sharpest prior-art hit on the 'prefixes cannot be certified independent of model' premise of C4 — under the existing name 'absence of model-agnostic traits'.
claims.quote: The above experiments demonstrate that the performance rankings of different prompts are inconsistent among different models. Furthermore, different models may suffer from different prompt variances. Therefore, it is unlikely to characterize the worst prompts using model-independent features.

claims.claim: Model RANKING is unstable under choice of phrasing: rankings derived from a single 'original' phrasing hold within a model family but correlate only weakly ACROSS families (Gemma vs Llama), which the authors say questions the validity of single-phrasing evaluation. This partially anticipates C1's ranking-flip component — but for accuracy/win-rate rankings, not for rankings on a structural readout like fixed-point fraction, and no Spearman values are reported.
claims.quote: the original performance serves as a reliable metric for ranking within the same model family, as it aligns well with the best, worst, and average performances. However, we find that this alignment weakly correlates when comparing across different model families, such as Gemma and Llama, questioning the methodological validity of using just one type of phrasing for a query to assess performance.

claims.claim: Varying only semantically-equivalent phrasing — same weights, same decoding, same evaluator — moves Llama-2-70B-chat's win-rate from 0.094 to 0.549 (a 45.5-point / 0.455 absolute swing), and scaling model size improves mean performance while slightly WORSENING robustness (std dev 0.133 -> 0.163 -> 0.156 for 7B/13B/70B). This establishes 'prompt dominates the readout' for accuracy, supporting-level pressure on C1's magnitude framing, but says nothing about prefix LENGTH non-monotonicity (C2) or direction reversal from a single raw value (C3).
claims.quote: the worst and best performance of Llama-2-70B-chat are 0.094 and 0.549, respectively, indicating a difference of 0.455. This suggests that the current LLMs' ability to follow instructions is not robust enough.

claims.claim: The paper argues AGAINST correctability rather than proposing a calibration: model-agnostic features are abandoned outright, model-dependent predictors fail (prompt perplexity shows positive and negative correlations nearly equally distributed; hidden-state probing is near chance 0.5; models self-assess at ~50-53% accuracy), and self-refinement prompt engineering DEGRADES performance (e.g. -15.52, -18.43 points). This is the closest hit on sub-question (e) — a published 'unpredictable in principle / cannot be corrected for' argument — though about worst-case accuracy, with no claim of in-principle impossibility for structural properties.
claims.quote: The above experiment results underscore that the worst prompt is almost unpredictable in advance without given the model.

result.publishDate: 2024-06-08 (arXiv v1; v4 revised 2024-10-30; published at NeurIPS 2024)

claims.claim: The SAME fixed prompt has opposite-signed / non-transferable effects across models: one permutation scores 88.7% on GPT2-XL (1.5B) and 51.6% (chance level) on GPT2-Large (0.8B), and pairwise Spearman correlations of permutation performance across models are near-zero and frequently NEGATIVE (Fig. 4 sample orderings: -0.35, -0.27, -0.26; Fig. 5 label orderings: -0.66, -0.54, -0.49). This is the closest published analogue to C4 — 'one fixed prefix helps some weights and hurts others' — but the measured quantity is downstream classification ACCURACY, not fixed-point/attractor structure of the model's own argmax map.
claims.quote: We find that a specific permutation's performance may drop from 88.7% to 51.6% by changing the underlying model from GPT2-XL (1.5B) to GPT2-Large (0.8B). This suggests that a particular permutation working well for one model does not imply that it will provide good results for another model. [...] If there is a common pattern for performant prompts, we should then be able to observe high correlation across models. However, the behaviour of permutations is seemingly random even across different sizes of the same model.

claims.claim: Prompts cannot be certified 'good' independently of the model — the paper states this as a headline finding in the abstract and quantifies it as a cross-model Spearman rank correlation of 0.05 between the 2.7B and 175B models, i.e. prompt RANKINGS are effectively uncorrelated across weights. This directly anticipates the 'prefixes cannot be certified safe independent of the model' half of C4, and the rank-correlation methodology (Spearman on a prompt/model grid) is the same instrument the claim set uses. It does NOT establish the converse direction of C1 (ranking of MODELS flipping under prefix change) — the correlation is over prompts, holding the model fixed.
claims.quote: We demonstrate that the order in which the samples are provided can make the difference between near state-of-the-art and random guess performance: essentially some permutations are "fantastic" and some not. We analyse this phenomenon in detail, establishing that: it is present across model sizes (even for the largest current models), it is not related to a specific subset of samples, and that a given good permutation for one model is not transferable to another. [...] the 175B and 2.7B model only has a correlation of 0.05, this means a good permutation for the 2.7B model is in no way guaranteed that it will also yield good performance for the 175B model.

claims.claim: The prompt effect is not monotone in prompt LENGTH (number of in-context examples): sweeping 1/2/4/8/16/32 shots, mean performance rises but the variance across orderings does not shrink and can grow. This partially anticipates C2's 'not a length effect' argument, though it is variance-across-permutations vs. shot count rather than a single scalar readout moving non-monotonically as one prefix is lengthened.
claims.quote: In Figure 3, we can observe that increasing the number of training samples leads to increases in performance. However, a high level of variance remains, even with a large number of samples and can even increase. Based on this, we draw the conclusion that order sensitivity is likely to be a fundamental issue of In-context Learning regardless of the number of training samples.

claims.claim: An existing calibration method (contextual calibration, Zhao et al. 2021) raises the mean but fails to remove prompt-induced variance — prior evidence that prompt effects on a model's behaviour are not correctable by output-distribution calibration. This partially pre-empts sub-question (e), though the paper argues only that THIS calibration is insufficient and then proposes its own mitigation (entropy-based prompt selection, +13% relative), so it stops short of claiming in-principle unpredictability.
claims.quote: An intuitive way to address this would be by calibrating the output distribution, along the lines of Zhao et al. (2021). However, we find that although calibration leads to much higher performance, the variance remains high (Figure 6, right).

claims.claim: The paper's only structural (non-accuracy) readout of prompt failure is collapse of the predicted label distribution — 'degenerate behaviour of bad prompts' — measured as label-histogram imbalance and prediction entropy. It never censuses fixed points, cycles, or attractors of a greedy/argmax self-feeding map, never iterates the model on its own output, and never varies a pre-loop conditioning prefix (its manipulation is the ORDER of in-context examples, all of which are task-formatted demonstrations). This bounds how far the paper pre-empts C1/C3 and leaves the fixed-point instrument itself untouched.
claims.quote: Degenerate behaviour of bad prompts We perform error analysis across performant and non-performant prompts and observe that the majority of failing prompts suffer from highly unbalanced predicted label distributions (Figure 6, left).

result.publishDate: 2021-04-18 (arXiv v1); v2 revised 2022-03-03; published at ACL 2022

claims.claim: The SAME template component is best for one model and among the worst for another — an explicit opposite-signed, cross-model prompt effect. Voronov et al. report that the output verbalizer "It was {}" ranks highest for Llama 2 70B under the DIRECT prediction method while being one of the worst for Falcon 40B. This is the strongest partial pre-emption of C4/C3 in the prompt-robustness literature, but the measured quantity is classification ACCURACY, not a structural/dynamical property, so it establishes the phenomenon 'prompt effects are model-specific and sign-flipping' under the existing name 'template non-transferability' without touching fixed-point structure.
claims.quote: Along with the non-transferability of whole templates, we notice that individual components also do not transfer both between models and prediction methods. For instance, while "It was {}" ranks highest among output verbalizers for Llama 2 70B with the DIRECT prediction method, it is one of the worst for Falcon 40B.

claims.claim: Prompt format changes alter the RANKING of models (not merely their scores), and the paper frames this as its headline framing device in Figure 1. This partially pre-empts the ranking-instability component of C1: 'a model RANKING flips under prefix change' is already an established result for accuracy-based rankings across 21 models and 4 classification datasets.
claims.quote: Figure 1: An example template transformation for two demonstrations. Different prompt formats lead to different rankings both for models and ICL methods, and the best template for one method can be suboptimal for others.

claims.claim: Cross-model transfer of best-performing templates is quantitatively low (IoU of top-10 templates exceeds 0.5 for only a few of 19 model pairs, and fails even within a single model family), and the authors state the general form of the C4 conclusion: a prompt cannot be certified good or bad independent of the model. This anticipates C4's REASONING while measuring a different quantity.
claims.quote: We observe that the IoU values exceed 0.5 only for a few model pairs on all datasets, meaning that the capacity for template transfer between models in the same setup is generally low. This is especially concerning for models within a single family: as these models are trained on the same data and have the same architecture, one would expect them to perform similarly on the same prompt formats. These observations signify that comparing ICL methods across models with a single template can lead to incorrect conclusions: a template that is effective for one model can easily be one of the worst choices for another model.

claims.claim: The magnitude of the format effect is extreme — a poor template drives the strongest models to random-guess level, and even the largest models show standard deviations across templates up to 35% of their mean score. This establishes that 'formatting dominates the readout' is already known for accuracy readouts, weakening the novelty of C1's magnitude framing (though C1's specific readouts — a discrete class label and fixed-point fraction moving 0.21 to 0.98 — are not accuracy).
claims.quote: We show that a poor choice of the template can reduce the performance of the strongest models and inference methods to a random guess level.

claims.claim: The paper does NOT threaten C2, C5, the BOS result, or the structural core of C4: a full-text search of the paper returns zero occurrences of fixed point, attractor, cycle, greedy/argmax decoding, degeneration, repetition, iterative/self-feeding probes, BOS/beginning-of-sequence, or attention sinks; it varies only in-context-learning template components (verbalizers, intra/inter separators) and measures only classification accuracy. On sub-question (e) it argues the OPPOSITE of C5's spirit — it proposes a correction (Template Ensembles) rather than arguing prompt effects are uncorrectable in principle.
claims.quote: As a first step towards mitigating this issue, we propose Template Ensembles that aggregate model predictions across several templates. This simple test-time augmentation boosts average performance while being robust to the choice of random set of templates.

result.publishDate: 2024-01-12 (arXiv v1); v3 revised 2024-06-06; published in Findings of ACL 2024

claims.claim: The same prompt condition has opposite-signed effects across different models: a prompt configuration that is optimal for one open-vocabulary detector degrades another badly. This is the paper's headline framing of prompt-model interaction, established across four detectors (YOLO World, SAM3, Grounding DINO, OWLv2) via one-factor-at-a-time analysis over eight prompt axes plus combinatorial search.
claims.quote: We decompose prompts into eight axes and conduct one-factor-at-a-time analysis followed by combinatorial optimization, revealing that models respond divergently to prompt structure: conditions that optimize one architecture can collapse another.

claims.claim: The paper asserts that a prompt cannot be certified as good independent of the model — optimal prompts are model-specific and cannot be guessed a priori — which is the same 'no model-independent prefix certification' structure as C4, stated for detection accuracy rather than for a structural readout.
claims.quote: Our findings demonstrate that prompt engineering can substantially close the gap between zero-shot VFMs and supervised detectors without requiring manual annotation, and that optimal prompts are model-specific, non-obvious, and transferable across domains.

claims.claim: The paper's response to model-specific prompt effects is to CORRECT for them by per-model search rather than to argue they are uncorrectable in principle: per-model combinatorial prompts produce large measured gains over a naive baseline (+0.357 mAP@0.5 for YOLO World, +0.362 for OWLv2 on synthetic cowpea flower data). It therefore does not support the 'unpredictable in principle / argue against calibration' position (sub-question e).
claims.quote: Applying model-specific combinatorial prompts yields substantial gains over a naive species-name baseline, including +0.357 mAP@0.5 for YOLO World and +0.362 mAP@0.5 for OWLv2 on synthetic cowpea flower data.

claims.claim: The measured quantity throughout is a benchmark accuracy metric (mAP@0.5) on zero-shot object detection in agricultural imagery — not a structural property of a model's own dynamics. The paper contains no iterative or self-feeding probe, no greedy/argmax map iteration, and no fixed-point, attractor, or cycle census; targeted extraction confirmed no such measurement.
claims.quote: We present a systematic prompt optimization framework evaluating four open-vocabulary detectors -- YOLO World, SAM3, Grounding DINO, and OWLv2 -- for cowpea flower and pod detection across synthetic and real field imagery.

claims.claim: The transferability result the paper reports is across DOMAINS and TASKS (synthetic-to-real, flower-to-pod), not across models: prompt structures discovered on synthetic data match or exceed those discovered on labeled real data for most model-object combinations (flower: 0.374 vs 0.353 for YOLO World; pod: 0.429 vs 0.371 for SAM3). Cross-model transfer is precisely what the paper reports as failing.
claims.quote: prompt structures optimized exclusively on synthetic data transfer effectively to real-world fields: synthetic-pipeline prompts match or exceed those discovered on labeled real data for the majority of model-object combinations (flower: 0.374 vs. 0.353 for YOLO World; pod: 0.429 vs. 0.371 for SAM3)

claims.claim: The paper's headline finding is that prompt components have model-specific, non-transferable effects across LLMs — the exact conceptual content of C4 ('the effect is not a property of the prefix'), stated in the abstract and named as 'model-specific inductive biases'. This is prior art for the CONCEPT of C4 under a different name, though measured on human-behavior-alignment indicators in a driving simulator rather than on fixed-point structure of an argmax map.
claims.quote: A systematic prompt ablation study reveals that prompt components act as model-specific inductive biases that do not transfer across LLMs.

claims.claim: One and the same single-factor prompt ablation (A2, removing the previous-acceleration-plan component) has an OPPOSITE-SIGNED effect on the two models' structural behavioral alignment: it raises o3 from 4/5 to 5/5 qualitative indicators (the paper's only 5/5 result alongside A7) while dropping Gemini 2.5 Pro from 4/5 to 2/5 (Table VI). Quantitatively the same ablation moves collision rate 0.00%->2.73% for o3 but 25.45%->16.36% for Gemini (Table VII). A7 (-Tactical plan) shows the same opposite pattern: o3 4/5->5/5, Gemini 4/5->3/5. This is the sharpest pre-emption of C4: one fixed prompt manipulation, opposite direction across weights, on a non-accuracy structural property.
claims.quote: Qualitative sensitivity. For o3, A6 (-Reassess) reduces tactical behavior alignment: merge-first probability no longer depends on projected headway. In contrast, A2 (-Prev. acc. plan) and A7 (-Tactical plan) improve o3's tactical alignment by restoring the human-like dependency on relative velocity advantage (5/5). Gemini 2.5 Pro is more sensitive to memory-related structure. A2 (-Prev. acc. plan) disrupts piecewise-linear velocities and weakens gap-related indicators, while A1 (-History) also degrades gap-related alignment.

claims.claim: The paper explicitly states the 'no prefix can be certified independent of the model' conclusion that C4 draws: across 7 ablations x 2 models, no prompt manipulation is uniformly beneficial, and each one produces model-specific tradeoffs. This is C4's normative consequence stated in prior work.
claims.quote: Across both models, no single ablation uniformly improves alignment with human behavior; instead, each removal reveals model-specific tradeoffs between qualitative alignment and safety performance.

claims.claim: The paper draws the general methodological prescription from the asymmetry — that prompt design does not transfer across model families and therefore behavioral claims about LLMs require structured prompt-sensitivity testing. It argues for MEASUREMENT (sensitivity testing), not for in-principle uncorrectability, so it does NOT pre-empt claim C5(e)-style 'unpredictable in principle' framing, but it does pre-empt the 'prompts cannot be certified safe across models' framing of C4.
claims.quote: These asymmetric effects mean that prompt design choices do not transfer across model families, arguing for structured sensitivity testing whenever behavioral claims about LLMs are made.

claims.claim: The instrument is an iterated self-feeding closed loop (the model's own prior output re-enters the next prompt under a receding horizon), and prompt structure is deliberately treated as a probe of behavioral structure — so the setup is genuinely an iterated-probe-plus-prefix-manipulation design. However, the readouts are behavioral-regression coefficients, collision rate, gap, and RMSE; the paper reports NO fixed-point, attractor, cycle, or BOS-token analysis, no model ranking, and n=2 models — so it does not touch C1's ranking claim, C2's non-monotonicity-in-length claim, or the fixed-point/attractor census itself.
claims.quote: The plan is executed under a receding horizon, after which the system re-queries the LLM with updated state. Both vehicles are controlled in parallel by independent LLM instances with mirrored observations.

result.publishDate: 2026-03-11 (arXiv v1); v2 revised 2026-05-18; to appear in IEEE ITSC 2026 proceedings

claims.claim: The paper defines and empirically measures a census-style readout over conditioning contexts for GREEDY decoding — the non-termination ratio r_L, i.e. the fraction of held-out contexts whose greedy continuation fails to terminate within L steps.
