This is the closest published ancestor of a 'fraction of starts that land in a degenerate/absorbing state' statistic for the argmax map, but it counts non-termination (length >= L), not fixed points or cycles of the map, and it is never framed dynamically.
claims.quote: r_L = 1/|D| ∑_{n=1}^{|D|} 𝟙(|Ŷ^(n)| ≥ L) ... We use L=1500, more than 10 times the max training sequence length.

claims.claim: The conditioning context is held FIXED at k=10 tokens throughout, and the authors explicitly report that different context distributions (train / valid / test / randomly generated) produced similar non-termination results — so the paper reports no prefix-dominance effect, runs no prefix-length sweep, and contains no prefix-type contrast. It therefore does not pre-empt the domain-dominance, non-monotone-in-length, or sign-flip claims; adversarially, it is a nearby prior measurement that found the opposite (context-insensitivity) under a much coarser prefix manipulation.
claims.quote: Unless specified otherwise, we report metrics using the test context distribution, since the train, valid, and randomly generated context distributions had similar results.

claims.claim: Under identical greedy decoding, the structural (non-accuracy) readout varies by more than an order of magnitude across models — tanh-RNN 12.35% ± 5.18, LSTM-RNN 1.53% ± 1.41, GPT-2 117M 37.91% non-termination. This establishes model-dependence of a degeneration statistic, i.e. the precondition for a prompt×model interaction claim, but the paper never crosses a fixed prefix with multiple models and so reports no opposite-signed prefix effect.
claims.quote: tanh-RNN with greedy: 12.35 ± 5.18%; LSTM-RNN with greedy: 1.53 ± 1.41%; GPT-2 117M with greedy (Table 4): 37.91%

claims.claim: The paper localizes the cause of degenerate infinite generation in the MODEL × DECODING-ALGORITHM pairing, not in the conditioning context — inconsistency is proved as a property of incomplete decoding algorithms applied to a model. The 'locus of the effect' framing in prior art is thus algorithm-centric, leaving the model × prefix locus unclaimed.
claims.quote: A consistent recurrent language model paired with an incomplete decoding algorithm can induce an inconsistent sequence distribution.

claims.claim: The paper connects its non-termination phenomenon to the neural-degeneration/repetition literature (Holtzman et al.), attributing some degenerate repetition to decoding inconsistency, and acknowledges that even a fixed-up sampler can enter a repetitive cycle — but it uses no dynamical-systems vocabulary (no 'attractor', no 'fixed point', no cycle census) and never enumerates or classifies the terminal states of the greedy map.
claims.quote: the examples suggest that some cases of degenerate repetition [Holtzman et al. 2019]; [Welleck et al. 2019] are attributed to inconsistency ... the sampling process can still enter a repetitive cycle (e.g., when the constant is close to 1), though it is guaranteed to terminate.

result.publishDate: 2020-02-06 (arXiv v1; published at ICLR 2020; latest revision 2020-10-02)

claims.claim: The paper attributes greedy-decoding repetition loops to a self-reinforcement effect that is MONOTONE and SATURATING in the number of prior repetitions — a single-signed, predictable attractor mechanism. This is the opposite shape from the target paper's C2 (non-monotone response in prefix token count) and C3/C4 (opposite-signed effects), so it does not pre-empt them; it is the closest published statement about greedy-decoding attractor formation.
claims.quote: 2) Self-reinforcement effect: the probability of repetition increases almost monotonically with the number of historical repetitions. Finally, the probability of repetition stabilizes around a certain ceiling value.

claims.claim: The paper DOES vary the content that conditions the model (three corpora: random-vocabulary tokens, BookCorpus, Wikitext-103) and finds that loop strength depends on that content — but it explains the dependence by a single monotone scalar predictor (initial sentence probability TP_0), i.e. it argues FOR calibratability of the effect. This directly answers sub-question (e) in the negative: no prior claim here that the effect is unpredictable in principle. The three corpora all move the SAME direction (all monotone increasing, differing only in magnitude/ceiling), so no opposite-sign result is reported.
claims.quote: We can find that the sentences with high initial sentence probability TP0, such as sentences sampled from Dwiki and Dbook, have a stronger self-reinforcement effect: TP and WR grows faster and reach the high ceiling values with a few repetitions.

claims.claim: All quantitative repetition analysis is conducted on exactly ONE model — a 16-layer, 750M-parameter Transformer decoder trained on Wikitext-103 — so the paper contains no cross-model comparison of conditioning effects and therefore cannot and does not report opposite-signed effects of the same prefix on different weights. C4 (one fixed 9-token prefix raising two models to ~1.0 while driving four others to ~0.0) is not anticipated here.
claims.quote: Following the previous work [35, 19], the pre-trained model is a 16-layer Transformer decoder trained on Wikitext-103.

claims.claim: The paper's Winner Rate (WR) metric is an argmax-based measure — it counts tokens that are the greedy argmax at their step, i.e. it measures whether a repeated string is locally fixed under the greedy map. This is the nearest published approach to fixed-point structure of the argmax map. However it is computed on manually constructed sequences where a supplied sentence is repeated N times, NOT by censusing where free-running trajectories from random starts terminate; no fixed-point fraction over a population of initial conditions is defined or measured.
claims.quote: We say xn,l is a winner if Pθ(xn,l|x<n,l) > Pθ(x0,l|x<0,l) and xn,l = arg max P(·|x<n,l). ... A higher winner rate means that the repetitions are more likely to be generated by a maximization-based decoding algorithm such as greedy decoding.

claims.claim: In this literature the prefix is treated as a nuisance variable to be AVERAGED OVER rather than as an explanatory factor: the headline degeneration statistics are means across many different Wikitext-103 dev-set prefixes at a fixed 50-token length, with no analysis of between-prefix variance and no variation of prefix length or type. This is evidence that the degeneration/repetition literature has not framed pre-loop conditioning as the dominant factor (supports novelty of C1).
claims.quote: The model results are the average of generated texts given different prefixes from the Wikitext-103 dev set. Specifically, given 50 tokens as the prefix, the model greedily generates the next 200 tokens.

result.publishDate: 2022-06-06 (v1); v2 2022-10-09; published at NeurIPS 2022 (36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)

claims.claim: The paper names and formalizes "Model Drifting": a prompt optimized for a source LLM is suboptimal on a target LLM. This is the closest existing NAME for the prompt-model interaction framing behind C1/C4, but it is defined purely over a task-performance metric A(.), with the headline instance being GPT-5's best HumanEval prompt scoring 99.39% on GPT-5 but 68.70% when moved to Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (whose own optimum is 79.47%).
claims.quote: Yet prompts are highly model-sensitive: reusing a prompt engineered for one model on another often yields substantially worse performance than a prompt optimized for the target model. We term this phenomenon Model Drifting.

claims.claim: The paper's cross-model transfer matrices show UNIFORMLY ONE-DIRECTIONAL degradation, not opposite-signed effects: every model's own prompt is its best prompt and transferring it only ever loses accuracy. It therefore does NOT report the same prefix raising one model and lowering another, which is exactly the C4 phenomenon; it reports only unshared optima, i.e. "merely unshared" in the paper's own C4 terminology.
claims.quote: In nearly all cases, the diagonal entries, where a model uses its own optimized prompt, achieve the highest accuracy, while transferring that prompt to other scales within the same family leads to substantial degradation (e.g., Llama3.1-70B-Instruct -> Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-32B -> Qwen3-8B).

claims.claim: Every readout in the paper is task accuracy on a benchmark; no structural, dynamical, or decoding-map quantity is measured anywhere. There is no measurement of fixed points, attractors, cycles, greedy/argmax iteration, self-feeding loops, BOS/beginning-of-sequence tokens, or model rankings under prompt change. It therefore bears on none of sub-questions (a), (b: fixed-point/attractor part), (d), or (f).
claims.quote: Evaluation Metric and Setup. We report average Pass@1 accuracy for all coding benchmarks, ... Verified benchmark, we instead report the resolved rate. For Terminal-Bench, we report the accuracy.

claims.claim: The paper argues the prompt-model interaction IS systematically correctable, not unpredictable in principle: it finds a shared latent direction in source->target prompt edits across tasks and builds a training-free mapping that recovers performance (relative gains of 27.39% on o3 and 15.79% on Llama-3.1-70B for SWE-Bench over direct transfer). This is the opposite stance to sub-question (e) and does not support any "cannot be certified / cannot be corrected for" prior art.
claims.quote: The consistently positive similarities reveal that source-to-target prompt transformations exhibit shared latent structures, suggesting the existence of a transferable pattern across tasks and thus supporting the feasibility of cross-task prompt transfer.

claims.claim: The paper credits MAPO (Chen et al., 2024) as the earlier work first establishing that prompt effectiveness is model-specific, making MAPO the earlier prior-art anchor for the general "prompts do not certify independent of the model" framing; and it reports drift within a single model family across scales at up to 50-70% relative loss on xCodeEval, i.e. the phenomenon is claimed to be broad but still accuracy-only.
claims.quote: Chen et al. (2024) introduce MAPO, a model-adaptive prompt optimizer that learns to tailor prompts for specific LLMs, showing that prompt effectiveness strongly depends on the underlying model family.

claims.claim: In iterated LLM transmission chains, the instruction/task given to the model (the pre-loop scaffold) has a strong, statistically significant, and clearly ordered effect on attractor STRENGTH, whereas the model effect is reported as weaker and less differentiated (only one model separates out). This is a conceptual partial pre-emption of C1's 'the conditioning dominates the loop readout' for an iterative self-feeding LM probe.
claims.quote: We find a strong effect of Task on attractor strength: Continue leads to significantly stronger attraction than Take Inspiration, itself leading to significantly stronger attraction than Rephrase. ... As for the effect of model, we observe significantly weaker attraction for Llama3-70b compared to GPT3.5, Llama3-8B and Mixtral-8x7b.

claims.claim: Under the SAME task/instruction, different models drift in OPPOSITE directions on a structural (non-accuracy) text property: text length shrinks on average for GPT3.5 and Llama3-8B while it grows for Mixtral-8x7B and GPT-4o-mini. This is the closest published analogue to C4 (same conditioning, opposite-signed structural effect across weights), though the sign flip is across models under a fixed task rather than across models under one fixed 9-token prefix, and the property is unbounded (length) rather than a bounded fixed-point fraction.
claims.quote: when looking at the evolution of texts length, using GPT3.5 or Llama3-8B leads text to become on average shorter, while using Mixtral-8x7B or GPT-4o-mini shifts the distribution towards greater lengths.

claims.claim: Model RANKING/selection flips depending on the evaluation protocol: a model preferred under single-step evaluation is not the preferred model under iterated (multi-step transmission) evaluation. This partially anticipates the 'ranking instability' component of C1, but the varying factor is single-step vs iterated evaluation, not the pre-loop prefix/domain.
claims.quote: One may therefore choose Mistral-7B based on single-step evaluation, even though Llama3-8B is the optimal choice for many applications.

claims.claim: Their 'attractor' is not a fixed point of a deterministic map but a fitted linear-regression equilibrium of a scalar text property (position l = I/(1-s) with convergence when |s|<1), estimated over 6 models x 3 tasks x 20 initial texts x 5 chains x 50 steps. There is no census of fixed points, no fixed-point fraction, and no discrete fixed-point class — bounding how much of the instrument (and of C1/C2's specific readouts) this paper can pre-empt.
claims.quote: attractors as the theoretical equilibrium point to which the iterated generation process may eventually converge ... position (i.e., the location in output generation space the process converges toward) and its strength (i.e., the intensity to which generated outputs are pulled toward it)

claims.claim: The chains are run with stochastic sampling (temperature 0.8, top_p 0.95), not greedy/argmax decoding, and the attractor framework presupposes that chains converge to the same attractor from a broad range of STARTING texts — i.e. the loop's seed is assumed to wash out. Neither the deterministic argmax map nor prefix-driven non-monotonicity (C2) nor BOS-token effects are examined, so this work does not pre-empt C2 or the BOS result.
claims.quote: Temperature was set to 0.8 with and top_p to 0.95. ... for a broad range of starting conditions, different variants of a given cultural trait will converge towards the same attractor

result.publishDate: 2024-07-05 (arXiv v1; published at ICLR 2025; v3 consulted)

claims.claim: The dynamical-systems framing of iterated LLM text-to-text mapping — explicitly including fixed points, limit cycles, basins of attraction, and periodic orbits — is established prior art as of Feb 2025. The paper defines T_{n+1} = P(T_n) over 1,000 seed sentences x 15 rounds and reports 2-period attractor cycles in all 8 models tested (per-model 2-periodicity degree tau: Llama3-70B 0.60, Mistral-7B 0.71, Llama3-8B 0.72, GPT-4o 0.81, GPT-4o-mini 0.83, Qwen2.5-7B 0.86, 14B 0.89, 72B 0.92). This pre-empts the ATTRACTOR/ITERATED-MAP FRAMING generically, but not any domain/prefix claim: the readout is a continuous edit-distance periodicity scalar, not a fixed-point FRACTION over random starts, and there is no discrete four-way class.
claims.quote: our study reveals that successive paraphrasing converges to stable periodic states, such as 2-period attractor cycles, limiting linguistic diversity. This phenomenon is attributed to the self-reinforcing nature of LLMs, as they iteratively favour and amplify certain textual forms over others. This pattern persists with increasing generation randomness or alternating prompts and LLMs.

claims.claim: The paper's headline conclusion is the DIRECT NEGATION of C1 (domain dominates) in its regime: it varies the prompt (four paraphrasing prompts randomly selected per iteration) and concludes the attractor structure is a property of the iterative transformation and NOT of the prompt. It therefore does not pre-empt C1 — it asserts the opposite null, and does so from a within-loop prompt-randomization design rather than a fixed pre-loop conditioning prefix held constant across a run.
claims.quote: For prompt variation, we design four different paraphrasing prompts (refer to Appendix C.2) and randomly select one at each iteration. Despite regularly switching prompts, the 2-period cycle persists... The system remains in a basin of attraction shared across these varied modeling conditions, implying that the stable cycle is a robust property of the iterative transformation rather than a quirk of any particular prompt or model.

claims.claim: On C4 (the central claim: same prefix, opposite-signed effects across models), this paper claims the reverse — that attractor states are model-independent and shared across weights. Crucially, this is asserted from model-ALTERNATION within one loop plus a cross-model perplexity check, NOT from a crossed prefix-by-model design; no experiment in the paper holds one prompt fixed and compares its signed effect across separate models. So C4 is not anticipated here, and this paper is the strongest 'adjacent but opposite-conclusion' citation to engage.
claims.quote: Interestingly, perplexity computed by a single model (e.g., Llama3-8B) on paraphrases generated by other models still decreases over iterations in Figure 6. This suggests that the attractor states are not confined to a single model's parameter space. Instead, they reflect a more general statistical optimum that multiple LLMs gravitate toward.

claims.claim: The paper does contain one measured prompt effect on a structural (non-accuracy) readout: swapping a simple paraphrase prompt for a 'complex' one lowers 2-periodicity from 0.80 to 0.67 and raises convergence perplexity from 1.19 to 1.33. This partially anticipates the weak form of 'prompt changes a structural attractor readout' — but only n=1 model (GPT-4o-mini), one direction of change, no ranking, no class flip, and the authors read it as a failure to move the structure. It does not touch C2 (non-monotonicity in prefix length) or C3 (bidirectional movement).
claims.quote: Although the sophisticated prompt alleviated the periodicity and convergence in some degree, the pattern of 2-period cycle remained strong. For context, a periodicity score of 0.67 implies an average edit distance of 0.33 between paraphrases two steps apart, whereas direct paraphrase exhibits an edit distance of 0.68.

claims.claim: The instrument is materially different from a token-level argmax map, which limits how much this can pre-empt anything: iteration is at the TEXT level via an instruction-conditioned paraphrase call under stochastic decoding with beam selection, not a deterministic short-window argmax over tokens. There is no greedy/argmax fixed-point census, no BOS-token experiment, no chat-template or system-prompt manipulation, and no reported proportion of trajectories terminating in a 1-period fixed point (only aggregate 2-periodicity). This answers sub-question (d) negatively for this source.
claims.quote: By default, we set the temperature to 0.6 and p to 0.9 during the decoding process. We sample 10 different paraphrases at each step by setting the number of search beams to 10 and sequentially rephrasing each sample for 15 rounds. We select the candidate with the highest probability for the next paraphrasing iteration.

claims.claim: Under one fixed minimal-input regime, the rate of degenerate (repetition-loop) output differs by 5.4x across model families — DeepSeek 1.9% vs Qwen 10.3% — establishing that repetition-attractor propensity is a per-model property under a held-constant prefix condition. This is a MAGNITUDE difference across models, not an opposite-signed effect of one prefix, so it anticipates the 'model-specific degeneration' half of C4 but not its sharp form (same prefix driving some models to ~1.0 and others to ~0.0 on the same readout).
claims.quote: In terms of degenerate ratio, DeepSeek produces degenerate text in only 1.9% of generations, whereas Qwen exhibits degeneration in 10.3% of its outputs, representing a 5.4-fold difference.

claims.claim: Removing the chat template from the pre-generation context materially changes a measured structural readout of the model's output distribution (PCA dispersion of representations, metaphor diversity), i.e. the chat-template-vs-bare-prefix contrast is shown to be a real experimental factor and not a nuisance — but the readout affected is representation dispersion and lexical diversity, not fixed-point fraction, fixed-point class, or model ranking.
claims.quote: Removing chat templates leads to more widely dispersed PCA representations and substantially more diverse metaphors.

claims.claim: The probe is stochastic free generation, not a deterministic map: sampling at temperature 1.0 with top-p 0.9, up to 4,096 tokens, 16,000 samples per model (256,000 total across 16 models), terminating on the token limit or a sampled EOS. Consequently no argmax/greedy map is iterated, no trajectory is censused for termination in a fixed point, and the paper contains no discussion of fixed points, attractors, or cycles of a decoding map — the degeneration statistic is a text-level repetition detector (a phrase >=10 characters repeated >=5 times consecutively covering >=5% of the output), not a fixed-point census.
claims.quote: the maximum token limit is reached or an end-of-sequence token is sampled

claims.claim: From topic-neutral seed prompts, each model family falls into a systematic and distinct content basin with quantified frequencies (GPT-OSS programming 27.1% and mathematics 24.6%; Llama literary 9.1%; DeepSeek religious content; Qwen multiple-choice questions), demonstrating strong weight-specific structure in near-unconstrained generation under a shared minimal input.
claims.quote: GPT-OSS predominantly generates programming (27.1%) and mathematical content (24.6%), whereas Llama most frequently generates literary content (9.1%). DeepSeek often generates religious content, while Qwen frequently generates multiple-choice questions.

claims.claim: The paper's motivating thesis is that the choice of conditioning prompt limits what can be observed about a model — an argument that prior measurements are scaffold-constrained — but it is framed as a coverage/observability limitation motivating minimal prompts, not as a claim that prompt effects on a structural property are unpredictable in principle or uncorrectable (relevant to sub-question e, which it does not answer affirmatively).
claims.quote: most existing analyses rely on topic- or task-specific prompts, which can substantially limit what can be observed

claims.claim: The paper holds the prompt/scaffold COMPLETELY FIXED across every condition it runs — the only varied parameters are decoding temperature and the seed corpus. It therefore performs no pre-loop conditioning manipulation of any kind and cannot pre-empt C1, C2, C3, or C4. Its single refinement prompt is printed verbatim in Appendix A and reused at every iteration.
claims.quote: Given an initial abstract V0 , we repeatedly apply the same refinement operator Rθ , implemented by an LLM under a fixed prompt and decoding configuration … All experiments use the same prompt and refinement horizon.

claims.quote: (2) Introducing one or two initial tokens doesn't fully restore model perplexity, showing that the model doesn't solely use the first token as the attention sink. (3) Introducing four initial tokens generally suffices; further additions have diminishing returns.

claims.quote: Language Models (LMs) assign significant attention to the first token, even if it is not semantically important, which is known as attention sink. ... we first demonstrate that attention sinks exist universally in LMs with various inputs, even in small models.

claims.claim: The SAME input manipulation produces qualitatively DIFFERENT structural outcomes across different model weights: repeated-token input destroys the attention sink in Mistral and LLaMA models while GPT2-XL retains a sink metric of 62.28%. claims.quote: With repeated tokens, attention sink in Mistral and LLaMA models disappears. In Appendix C.1, we prove that for LMs with NoPE/relative PE/ALiBI/Rotary, if the first T tokens are the same, their corresponding hidden states are the same.

claims.claim: The sink is a property of ABSOLUTE POSITION and of the training data distribution, not of the BOS token's identity: randomizing the initial token shifts the sink to the second token (Sink2 = 14.08%), and fixing an arbitrary token at position 2 or 3 during pre-training relocates the sink to that token. This means a BOS-specific effect on downstream dynamics cannot be attributed to BOS semantics, and correspondingly this literature does not predict which direction a BOS prefix would push any decoding-level readout.
claims.quote: fixing the token 𝒙fix in the second/third token position during pre-training. Consequently, the attention sink always appears in the fixed token instead of the first token.

claims.claim: The paper's central mechanistic conclusion is that the sink is a no-op key bias that absorbs attention mass WITHOUT contributing to value computation — which argues that the first/BOS token's large attention share is largely non-informative. This cuts AGAINST attention-sink work pre-empting a claim that a BOS token substantially changes the model's output map, since the sink literature's own account predicts minimal effect on computed values.
claims.quote: attention sink acts more like key biases, storing extra attention and meanwhile not contributing to the value computation.

claims.claim: The paper measures attention distributions only; it performs no evaluation of generation, decoding, downstream behavior, repetition, fixed points, attractors, or iterated/self-feeding maps, and explicitly disclaims knowledge of downstream consequences. Therefore it does not pre-empt any claim about fixed-point fraction, fixed-point class, attractor census, or model ranking under prefix variation.
claims.quote: it remains unclear whether attention sink benefits LM downstream performance

This is the closest published precedent for 'one BOS token is a massive, discrete intervention on model behavior', but the readout is task accuracy, not fixed-point/attractor structure of an iterated argmax map.
claims.quote: We find that removing the attention sink (i.e., removing the ⟨bos⟩ token) in Gemma 7B at inference time consistently lowers the performance, and this drop is particularly pronounced on the long-context ruler benchmark – in accordance with our prediction that attention sinks are particularly useful for long-context. We highlight that our results suggest that one should take great care in how the ⟨bos⟩ token is handled at inference, as the model's predictive capabilities seem to be greatly impacted, especially in the long-context regime.

claims.claim: The paper gives a mechanism by which a single first-position token controls the model's whole internal dynamics: the BOS sink slows information mixing and limits how far a perturbation of the prompt propagates; removing BOS in Gemma 7B makes attention maps much smoother and sharply increases the Jacobian norm ||J_ij||, i.e. perturbation spread. This supplies a mechanistic explanation for why a BOS prefix could shift a downstream dynamical readout, without measuring any such readout.
claims.quote: The presence of attention sinks slows down the mixing of information between tokens and hence makes Transformers more robust to perturbations of prompts. ... The presence of a sink draws attention away from the rest of the tokens, limiting the spread of perturbed information and resulting in more stable embeddings.

claims.claim: Whether a model depends on the BOS token is model-specific and determined by the pretraining recipe: dropping BOS at inference reduces the sink metric from 90.84% to 0.05% (valid loss 2.69 -> 7.56) for a model trained with fixed BOS, but leaves a model trained without BOS essentially unaffected (65.10% -> 65.15%, loss 2.69 -> 2.70). The same prefix intervention thus has wildly different MAGNITUDES across weights — but the paper reports no case of OPPOSITE-SIGNED effects, so it does not pre-empt the C4 sign-flip claim.
claims.quote: if the model is trained with ⟨bos⟩ always appearing at the first token, removing ⟨bos⟩ during inference removes the attention sink, i.e. the model relies on the ⟨bos⟩ token to form the sink. Instead, if there is no ⟨bos⟩ during training, the sink forms at the first token regardless, but is slightly weaker. Removing ⟨bos⟩ in a model that was trained with ⟨bos⟩ present greatly reduces performance.

claims.claim: The leverage that the first token exerts over mixing scales systematically with model size and pretraining context length: LLaMa 3.1 sink metric (eps=0.8) rises 45.97 (8B) -> 73.49 (70B) -> 78.29 (405B), and models pretrained at context 128 form essentially no sinks while those at 1024/2048 reach ~37-38%. This means the magnitude of any BOS/prefix effect is expected a priori to be model-dependent, weakening the surprise value of cross-model heterogeneity in prefix effects (partially relevant to C1/C4) while still not addressing direction.
claims.quote: after pre-training, the attention sinks indeed seem to be much more prevalent for models trained on longer contexts, and nearly non-existent for very short-context-trained models

claims.claim: All convergence/collapse dynamics analysed in the paper are DEPTH-WISE (rank collapse, representational collapse, over-smoothing, convergence to 'pure mixing' as layers stack), never token-wise autoregressive dynamics. The paper contains no census of fixed points, cycles, or attractors of a greedy/argmax next-token map, and never iterates a decoding map to convergence — so it cannot pre-empt the fixed-point-fraction or fixed-point-class readouts, only the BOS-matters-a-lot premise behind them.
claims.quote: The key intuition is that attention matrices 'mix' information, and repeated mixing converges to a space that is uninformative. ... Importantly, Veličković et al. (2024) proved that, when generalising to sufficiently longer contexts at inference time, global attention matrices cannot remain sharp, and will therefore always converge to "pure mixing".

I verified this against the Figure 1 rank columns: Llama2-7b-chat sits at rank 10 in the original ranking and at rank 2 under the "Fixed Answer (B)" perturbation — an 8-position move. 3) "normalized Kendall's tau falling to 0.455-0.564" — CONFIRMED, and the range is well-chosen rather than cherry-picked. Definition verified: "we measure the normalized Kendall's tau distance... We report ktau = (tau+1)/2, where ktau = 1.0 indicates total agreement between rankings, and ktau = 0 indicates complete disagreement by reversing the original rankings" — so "normalized Kendall's tau" is the paper's own term. ktau = 0.564: choice-order shuffling (Table 1), with narrative "5 out of 11 models change in ranking after the perturbation and ktau drops to 0.564." ktau = 0.455: Table 2 kappa-tau row ("- 0.455 0.527 0.527 0.855") for fixing the correct answer to each position. Lower values do exist in the paper (0.382, 0.164) but they belong to Table A.26 "Providing the incorrect answer in-context" — an in-context knowledge manipulation that is NOT semantically neutral. So restricting the cited range to 0.455-0.564 for semantically-neutral format perturbations is precise, not an overreach.

4) Perturbation list ("answer-choice order, choice symbols, scoring method") — CONFIRMED: "Shuffling/changing the presented order of the choices, swapping choice symbols, and alternative scoring methods all cause major shifts to the rankings (determined by thresholding ktau <= 0.75)." We report ktau = (tau+1)/2, where ktau = 1.0 indicates total agreement between rankings, and ktau = 0 indicates complete disagreement." Figure 1 reports ktau for each perturbed ranking vs. the original. This is the single most important omission: C1's ranking component is a Spearman +0.400/+0.300 against a 0.6 concordance gate, and this paper measures exactly rank-correlation instability of a model leaderboard under prefix/format change with a normalized-agreement statistic on the same [0,1] scale — "changes in rankings up to 8 positions" (abstract). By asserting the source has no ranking metric, the claim materially UNDERSTATES the pre-emption threat to C1, which is the opposite of what an adversarial prior-art gate should do.

(3) Additionally under-reported re C4: Table 1 (order-of-choices perturbation, one fixed perturbation across 11 models) reports OPPOSITE-SIGNED effects on the SAME quantity: dAcc = +6.0 (Llama2-13b-chat), +1.0 (Mistral-7b), +0.7 (Llama2-13b), +0.3 (Llama2-70b-chat) vs -8.3 (Yi-6b), -5.0 (Llama2-7b, Yi-34b), -3.0 (phi-2); dRStd likewise +7.4 (phi-2) vs -6.2 (Llama2-70b-chat). It is unclear how benchmarking prompt choices advantage/disadvantage different models"; "Some models elicit this behavior much more strongly ... Other models in the same size range are more stable." The only "BOS" substring hit is "Maarten Bosma", a surname in the references. The paper does use the LM Evaluation Harness (Gao et al., 2023). So the conclusion "cannot pre-empt the fixed-point/attractor structural readout in C1-C4" is SOUND and survives.

FALSE #1 — "entire measurement apparatus is a single-forward-pass log-likelihood comparison over four answer-letter tokens." The paper explicitly defines THREE scoring methods in Sec 3.2 and treats switching among them as a headline perturbation: "Symbol scoring: ... likelihood scores for the answer choice symbol"; "Hybrid scoring: ... likelihood scores for the answer choice content normalized by length"; "Cloze scoring: Prompt templates are structured..." (Fig. 3: "Cloze scoring does not [share the prompt]"). Hybrid and cloze score multi-token answer CONTENT, not four letter tokens, and require per-candidate passes, not a single forward pass. Figure 7 compares "{symbol, cloze, hybrid}" head-to-head; line 439 lists "alternative scoring methods" among the perturbations that cause ranking shifts.

MISREAD OF THE QUOTE — the supporting quote is verbatim accurate but describes the HARNESS'S DEFAULT MMLU BASELINE, not the paper's apparatus: "using the LM Evaluation Harness (Gao et al., 2023) library. THEIR implementation of MMLU measures the log-likelihood of each of the answer tokens ['A','B','C','D']...". That is the baseline the paper then perturbs away from. Using it to characterize the paper's "entire measurement apparatus" inverts its scope.

FALSE #2 — "its only metrics are dAcc and RStd." The paper reports a THIRD and arguably headline metric, normalized Kendall's tau distance between model rankings: "To measure the change in ranking induced by an applied perturbation to a benchmark, we measure the normalized Kendall's tau distance between two rankings of n models (Kendall, 1938) ... we report ktau = (tau+1)/2, where ktau = 1.0 indicates total agreement between rankings, and ktau = 0 indicates complete disagreement." Figure 1 reports ktau under each new ranking; the abstract reports "changes in rankings up to 8 positions"; result tables carry a Rank column (e.g. "Llama2-7b-chat (9→10)").

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE GATE: erasing Kendall's tau causes the claim to UNDERSTATE the threat to C1. The claim dismisses the overlap as merely "the ranking-instability framing," but this is a quantified rank-correlation result on model rankings under prefix/format change — the same structure as C1's Spearman +0.400/+0.300 against a 0.6 concordance gate, with a comparable pre-registered agreement threshold. That is a substantive partial pre-emption of C1's ranking sub-claim, not a framing. The claim's own internal inconsistency (denying a ranking metric exists while conceding the ranking framing) is the tell.

NOT outdated (ACL 2024, directly on point), not marketing, primary source quality is adequate. Refuted because the characterization is materially inaccurate in a direction that biases the novelty gate toward "novel."

Two of the claim's three factual premises are contradicted by the source's own text, and neither is supported by the offered quote (which describes the LM-Eval-Harness DEFAULT that the paper's whole point is to VARY, not the paper's apparatus).

(1) "entire measurement apparatus is a single-forward-pass log-likelihood comparison over four answer-letter tokens" — FALSE. Alzahrani et al. (arXiv:2402.01781, "When Benchmarks are Targets: Revealing the Sensitivity of Large Language Model Leaderboards", v2 3 Jul 2024) define and run THREE scoring methods, and "the method of answer selection" is one of its named perturbation axes (in the abstract). Verbatim: symbol scoring = "The model chooses the answer based on the likelihood scores for the answer choice symbol"; hybrid scoring = "likelihood scores for the answer choice content normalized by length"; cloze scoring = "Prompt templates are structured as a question followed by a single answer choice. Maximum normalized likelihood scores over all answer choices define the prediction." Cloze scoring constructs a SEPARATE prompt per choice (N forward passes, not one) and scores full answer-text continuations, not letter tokens. Further: the symbol-replacement perturbation swaps A/B/C/D for ["$","&","#","@"] and ["œ","§","Ze","ü"], and the paper also evaluates ARC-Challenge, which it states has "3-5 answer choices" — so "four answer-letter tokens" is wrong on both the token identity and the cardinality. The offered quote ("Their implementation of MMLU measures the log-likelihood of each of the answer tokens ['A','B','C','D']") says "Their" = EleutherAI's harness baseline; generalizing it to the paper's "entire measurement apparatus" is a misread of the control condition as the whole design.

(2) "its only metrics are dAcc and RStd" — FALSE. The paper also defines and reports ΔRStd ("change in bias") and Kendall's τ / normalized kτ ("computes the number of swapped pairs between two rankings normalized by the total number of pairs n(n−1)/2"; "kτ=1.0 indicates total agreement between rankings"). kτ is the paper's headline instrument — it is the rank-agreement statistic behind "changes in rankings up to 8 positions", i.e. exactly the ranking/concordance measurement the verifier's C1 uses a Spearman 0.6 concordance gate for. Omitting it understates the pre-emption threat rather than merely mislabelling it.

(3) Only the negative half survives: full-text search across two independent fetches (arxiv/html/v2 and ar5iv) returns no instances of "greedy", "generate/generation", "iterate", "fixed point", or "BOS", and no experiment feeds model output back as input. So "never iterates the model on its own output / no fixed points, attractors, cycles / no BOS analysis" is CONFIRMED, and the ultimate conclusion (cannot pre-empt the fixed-point/attractor readout) is probably right.

(4) The closing scope clause "only the ranking-instability framing" is also too narrow. RStd/ΔRStd is a NON-accuracy, non-benchmark structural property of the output distribution (selection bias), and the paper reports model-specific bias directions (Table 2: some models favor position A, others C or D; Yi-6b moves 3rd→7th/8th under perturbations while Mistral-7b/Llama2-7b shift ≤2 ranks). That is a prompt×model interaction with model-dependent sign on a structural quantity — the precise "already known under another name" hazard flagged for C3/C4 — so the source touches more than ranking instability, even though it never touches iterated-map structure.

Net: the claim is directionally right about the fixed-point gap but is an overreach on "entire" and "only", both contradicted by primary text, and it under-reports the source's kτ ranking metric and its non-accuracy RStd axis, which are the parts that actually bear on C1/C3/C4.

QUOTE FIDELITY: VERIFIED VERBATIM. Paper is "On the Worst Prompt Performance of Large Language Models" (Cao, Cai, Zhang, Zou, Lam; CUHK + Tencent AI Lab + PKU), arXiv:2406.10248v4, 30 Oct 2024. The supporting quote appears word-for-word at lines 230-235 of the extracted text: "The original performance assessment only provides a narrow perspective of a model's overall performance. Specifically, the original performance serves as a reliable metric for ranking within the same model family, as it aligns well with the best, worst, and average performances. However, we find that this alignment weakly correlates when comparing across different model families, such as Gemma and Llama, questioning the methodological validity of using just one type of phrasing for a query to assess performance."

NO MISREAD. I checked the immediately preceding context (lines 227-229) to test the most likely misreading — that the passage ranks PROMPTS, not MODELS. It does not: the preceding sentences compare Gemma-7b vs Gemma-2b (avg 0.31 vs 0.153) and Llama-2-7B/13B/70B (0.195/0.24/0.292), i.e. ranking models within a family. The claim's reading is correct.

EACH HEDGE IN THE CLAIM IS INDEPENDENTLY TRUE:
(1) "for accuracy/win-rate rankings" — correct. The metric is weighted win-rate against GPT-4 as reference/evaluator (AlpacaEval-derived, RobustAlpacaEval); 0.5 = parity with reference. "Win-rate" is exact; "accuracy" is the looser alternative offered, and the paper reserves "accuracy" for its hidden-state probing classifier.
(2) "no Spearman values are reported" — literally true. grep -i "spearman" over the full text returns ZERO hits. The paper reports Kendall's W and Pearson instead.
(3) "not for rankings on a structural readout like fixed-point fraction" — confirmed. grep for fixed.point|attractor|cycle|greedy|argmax|self-feed|degenerat returns nothing relevant (only one incidental "This process can be iterative" at line 126, about prompt-engineering pipelines). The paper never touches decoding dynamics.
(4) "authors say questions the validity of single-phrasing evaluation" — verbatim ("questioning the methodological validity of using just one type of phrasing").

MATERIAL ADDITION THE CLAIM UNDERSTATES (raises, not lowers, the threat to C1): the claim says no Spearman values are reported, which is true but may read as "no rank-correlation numbers at all." The paper DOES report a concordance statistic — Kendall's W (coefficient of concordance), Table 2: Llama family 0.443, Gemma family 0.548, all models 0.238 — with a banding scheme (Negligible <0.1, Weak 0.1-0.3, Moderate 0.3-0.5, Strong >=0.5). This is directly adjacent to C1's "0.6 concordance gate." Caveat: those W values quantify agreement of PROMPT rankings across models, a different quantity from the model-ranking claim in the quote (the cross-family model-ranking weakness is asserted qualitatively, with no number). The claim does not conflate the two, so this is not an error — but the prior-art gate should note that a concordance-based ranking-instability analysis already exists in this paper.

SOURCE QUALITY / RECENCY: primary source, arXiv preprint with public data and code (github.com/bwcao/RobustAlpacaEval), academic authorship, includes negative results (prompt-engineering and consistency methods fail to help). Not marketing, not a press release, not forum speculation. Claim strength is modest and hedged, so source strength is more than sufficient. The "outdated" test does not apply: this is a prior-art claim, and 2024 prior art does not expire against an unpublished 2026 paper — age makes it MORE threatening, not less.

VERIFIED AGAINST PRIMARY SOURCE (full PDF read, arXiv:2104.08786v2, 3 Mar 2022; published ACL 2022 main conf, long paper; Lu, Bartolo, Moore, Riedel, Stenetorp).

1. QUOTE IS VERBATIM, NOT PARAPHRASED. Page 3, boldface section head "Performant prompts are not transferable across models": "We find that a specific permutation's performance may drop from 88.7% to 51.6% by changing the underlying model from GPT2-XL (1.5B) to GPT2-Large (0.8B). This suggests that a particular permutation working well for one model does not imply that it will provide good results for another model. To validate this hypothesis, we use all possible order permutations of the four samples as prompts -- 24 in total. We then perform prediction conditioned on each of these prompts for different models and calculate the pairwise Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between the scores. These results are shown in Figure 4. If there is a common pattern for performant prompts, we should then be able to observe high correlation across models. However, the behaviour of permutations is seemingly random even across different sizes of the same model." Every element of the claim's quote appears word-for-word. Not a misread.

2. FIGURE 4 VALUES CHECKED CELL-BY-CELL. Caption: "Training sample permutation performance correlation across different models." Matrix over GPT2 0.1B/0.3B/0.8B/1.5B and GPT3 2.7B/6.7B/13B/175B. All three cited values verify and are in fact the three MOST negative cells: -0.35 (175B vs 0.8B), -0.27 (2.7B vs 1.5B), -0.26 (6.7B vs 0.3B). Off-diagonal cells are overwhelmingly near-zero/negative (-0.24, -0.24, -0.23, -0.22, -0.17, -0.14, -0.12, -0.11, -0.10, -0.09, -0.07, 0.01, 0.04, 0.05, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12, 0.13, 0.19, 0.20, 0.27). Figure 5 ("Training label pattern permutation performance correlation across different models"): -0.66 (175B vs 1.5B) VERIFIES; -0.49 VERIFIES and recurs 5+ times (6.7B row vs 0.1B/0.8B/2.7B/13B, 2.7B vs 6.7B). Figure 5 also contains strong POSITIVE cells the claim omits: +0.77 (175B vs 6.7B) and +0.71 (2.7B vs 0.1B), which cut against a clean "anti-correlated" reading. 4. THE SCOPE CAVEAT IS ACCURATE, which is what limits the claim's pre-emptive force. Table 2 confirms the measured quantity is downstream classification ACCURACY across eleven text-classification datasets (SST-2, SST-5, DBPedia, MR, CR, MPQA, Subj, TREC, AGNews, RTE, CB). Figures 4/5 correlate permutation ACCURACY SCORES. Nothing in the paper censuses fixed points, attractors, cycles, or any structure of the model's own greedy/argmax map. The claim states this limitation itself and does not overreach into the C4 target.

The claim says "opposite-signed"; the authors say "seemingly random" and "not transferable" -- absence of correlation, not a systematic sign inversion. Given the +0.77 and +0.71 cells in Fig 5, "seemingly random" is the better characterization of the correlation matrices. The genuine sign-flip evidence is the single 88.7% -> 51.6% (near-SOTA -> chance) same-permutation datapoint, which does support "one fixed prefix helps some weights and hurts others." The claim hedges correctly with "opposite-signed / non-transferable."

6. SOURCE QUALITY AND CURRENCY. Primary, peer-reviewed, top-tier venue (ACL 2022); not a preprint-only, press release, blog, or forum post; not a marketing or cherry-picked benchmark claim -- the negative-transfer result is presented as a PROBLEM the authors then work to overcome, i.e. it argues against their own method's convenience, which is the opposite of cherry-picking. Age is not a defect here: for a PRIOR-ART gate on an unpublished paper, a 2021/2022 date strengthens rather than weakens the claim's force. Found no basis to call it contradicted; later prompt-transferability work (e.g. soft-prompt transfer) concerns continuous prompts and does not overturn this discrete-permutation finding.

VERBATIM QUOTE IS GENUINE — the claim is not fabricated. arXiv:2604.09920 exists: "Does Your VFM Speak Plant? The Botanical Grammar of Vision Foundation Models for Object Detection" (Lundqvist, Ranario, Kamangir, Yun, Diepenbrock, Bailey, Earles; cs.CV; 2026-04-10). Raw abstract via export.arxiv.org contains the supporting quote character-for-character: "We decompose prompts into eight axes and conduct one-factor-at-a-time analysis followed by combinatorial optimization, revealing that models respond divergently to prompt structure: conditions that optimize one architecture can collapse another." Four detectors (YOLO World, SAM3, Grounding DINO, OWLv2), OFAT + combinatorial search: all confirmed.

REFUTED ON THREE GROUNDS:

(1) "ESTABLISHED" IS FALSE — the paper never ran the experiment. Full-text probe of the combinatorial/discussion sections: "The authors did not investigate whether optimal prompts for one detector harmed performance in others." No cross-model prompt transfer was tested. A separate probe of the OFAT results found per-axis deltas are not tabulated (Phase 1 results live in Figure 1 spider plots) and reported deltas are "same-sign but varying in magnitude." The phrase "conditions that optimize one architecture can collapse another" appears ONLY in the abstract, never in the body. The body-level evidence is INSENSITIVITY and MAGNITUDE HETEROGENEITY, not sign inversion: "Grounding DINO is largely insensitive to prompt elaboration beyond the bare noun 'flower'" (S3.1); "OWLv2 shows an unusual sensitivity to phenology terms" (S3.1); "YOLO World benefits most from prompts with full text negation" (S3.2); "For OWLv2 and Grounding DINO, emoji combinations did not outscore non-emoji configurations" (Table 4 note). "Did not outscore" and "largely insensitive" are ≤ and ≈0 — they are NOT "degrades another badly." The strong empirical proposition (optimal-for-A is harmful-to-B) is abstract-level promotional framing, unsupported by any reported measurement.

(2) "HEADLINE FRAMING" IS AN OVERREACH. The abstract's own emphasis marker "Crucially" attaches to synthetic-to-real prompt transfer, not to divergence. The closing sentence frames the contribution as "prompt engineering can substantially close the gap between zero-shot VFMs and supervised detectors without requiring manual annotation, and that optimal prompts are model-specific, non-obvious, and transferable across domains." Divergence is a supporting observation motivating model-specific optimization, not the headline.

(3) DOES NOT PRE-EMPT C4 EVEN AT FULL STRENGTH — domain and metric mismatch. The metric is mAP@0.5, a task-ACCURACY benchmark score on vision open-vocabulary detectors. Research question (c) explicitly demands a STRUCTURAL, "non-accuracy, non-benchmark" property. There is no iterated map, no self-feeding loop, no fixed point, attractor, or cycle census, and no language-model decoding dynamics anywhere in this work. At best it instantiates the generic, already-well-known "prompt-model interaction on task performance"; it says nothing about opposite-signed effects on a structural invariant of a model's own argmax map. C4's sharp form (one fixed 9-token prefix driving two models to ~1.0 and four to ~0.0 in fixed-point fraction) is untouched by this paper.

Body check of the HTML confirms it proposes a practical discovery procedure and makes no in-principle non-certifiability argument. C4's force is that prefixes CANNOT be certified; this paper's force is that good prompts CAN be found cheaply and reused. That is question (e) answered NO, not YES.

(2) THE SUPPLIED QUOTE DOES NOT SUPPORT THE SIGN-REVERSAL STRUCTURE. "Optimal prompts are model-specific, non-obvious, and transferable across domains" says only that the ARGMAX prompt differs per model — fully compatible with every prompt helping every model by differing amounts. That is banal per-model hyperparameter tuning, not C4's opposite-signed effect of ONE FIXED prefix. The only sentence with sign-reversal flavor ("models respond divergently to prompt structure: conditions that optimize one architecture can collapse another") is NOT the quote cited, and the body's concrete instantiation is a magnitude contrast, not a sign flip: OWLv2 gains +0.469 mAP from phenology terms while Grounding DINO is "largely insensitive to prompt elaboration" (insensitive ≠ opposite direction). No same-prompt-helps-A/hurts-B pair is demonstrated. Note also the same cited sentence ends with "transferable across domains," and the paper's headline transfer results are positive (synthetic→real: flower 0.374 vs 0.353 YOLO World; pod 0.429 vs 0.371 SAM3) — the quote is partly a transferability-SUCCEEDS claim.

(3) OFF-TARGET FOR THE GATE AS FRAMED. Every readout is mAP@0.5 detection accuracy on cowpea flowers/pods across four open-vocabulary vision detectors (YOLO World, SAM3, Grounding DINO, OWLv2). No autoregressive LM, no iterated/self-feeding decoding, no BOS token, no fixed points/attractors/cycles — confirmed absent in the body. The prior-art question (c) explicitly asks for opposite-signed effects on a STRUCTURAL, non-accuracy, non-benchmark property; this is precisely the accuracy/benchmark category the question carves out. Text strings used as open-vocabulary class queries to a detector are also not "pre-loop conditioning prefixes" of an autoregressive map.

WHAT SURVIVES (narrower, and the claim should be rewritten to this if kept): the conceptual shape "prompt-model interaction, with a prompt that optimizes one architecture degrading another" is already published in the vision open-vocabulary-detection literature as of April 2026. That mildly softens the framing novelty of C4's rhetoric, but does not touch C4's substance (fixed-point structure of an LM's greedy map, one fixed 9-token Pile prefix driving two models to ~1.0 and four to ~0.0). Threat level to C4: low. It is not "C4 already known under another name."

TWO REAL DEFECTS, neither flipping the verdict:
(1) "Headline finding" is an overreach. The title/headline is whether general-purpose LLMs can serve as human driver behavior models; the ablation is the 4th result sentence of the abstract and a subsidiary section (III-B). (2) The measured property is human-behavior-ALIGNMENT (goodness-of-fit to a human reference dataset, checkmark tallies + collision/gap/RMSE), i.e. closer in kind to accuracy/benchmark fit than to a structural property of the model's own map. The prior-art gate's question (c) specifically asks for a STRUCTURAL, non-accuracy property. The claim under review DISCLOSES this gap explicitly ("measured on human-behavior-alignment indicators in a driving simulator rather than on fixed-point structure of an argmax map"), so it is honestly scoped rather than misleading.
